title: Soil geochemical patterns in Lesvos island UNESCO Global Geopark, Greece: Unveiling the influence of diverse geology
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 205 Author(s): Efstratios Kelepertzis, Artemios Roussos, Christos Drougas, Zacharenia Kypritidou, Emmanouil Vassilakis, Nikolaos Zouros
abstract: A regional soil geochemical survey was carried out on the island of Lesvos, NE Aegean Sea, Greece, using an average density of 1 sample/25 km2 with the aim to investigate the geochemical variability of major and trace elements. The island encompasses a variety of rock and mineralisation types, including the Lesvos petrified forest, a well-documented geosite of international scientific importance, providing an opportunity to study how variations in lithology and hydrothermal mineralisation impact on elemental soil geochemistry. In total, 66 soil samples (0-20 cm depth) were collected across the entire island and the <2 mm fraction analysed for a variety of elements following a hot aqua regia digestion. In addition, 28 rock samples were also collected and analysed to assist in the interpretation of the soil geochemical patterns. The soil geochemical data were processed by multivariate statistical methods (factor and hierarchical cluster analysis) and Geographic Information System methods. The procedures used enabled the identification of several soil geochemical patterns that correlate with known rock types and mineralisation occurring on the island. Specific major and trace elements (Ba, Ca, Cd, Co, Cr, Fe, K, Na, Mg, Mn, Ni, Sr, Zn) exhibit pronounced concentration changes across the major lithological units, with median concentrations displaying orders of magnitude differences between the soil developed over different lithologies. A suite of trace elements (As, Cu, Mo, Pb, Sb) in soil fingerprint the hydrothermal mineralisation, exhibiting geochemical anomalies around known epithermal and porphyry-style deposits. No major diffuse anthropogenic contamination by potentially toxic elements appears to have affected the soil at the sampling density of 1 sample/25 km2. It is concluded that the applied soil sampling density has effectively mapped the regional patterns of the geochemical landscape of Lesvos island, with broader implications for geochemical mapping in similar regions characterized by lithological diversity.

title: An exploration of groundwater chromium contamination from a chromite mine, Sukinda, India
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 205 Author(s): Angus Fotherby, Biswajit Panda, Arka Chakraborty, Kit Baker, Sara Crozier, Ramananda Chakrabarti, Alexandra V. Turchyn
abstract: Chromium in the oxidised (hexavalent) form, Cr(VI), is an environmental contaminant due to its solubility and its associated health risks, both as a toxin and as a carcinogen. Sampling of surface and groundwaters, complemented by reactive transport modelling was conducted to explore chromium contamination associated with chromite mining in Sukinda Valley, Odisha, India. When in its reduced form, Cr(III), it is less toxic and readily precipitates into mineral forms, limiting its transport. We use field sampling, laboratory analyses, and numerical modelling to assess the extent, controls, and dynamics of chromium contamination and to evaluate potential natural attenuation and remediation strategies. Groundwater samples from wells and surface waters within and around Sukinda Valley have significant geochemical variability. Surface waters in the valley exhibit high Cr(VI) concentrations (up to 0.2 ppm), whereas deeper groundwater accessed via pump wells have negligible Cr(VI) and elevated Fe2+ and Mn2+, indicating naturally reducing conditions. Reactive transport modelling demonstrates that microbially-mediated dissimilatory iron reduction drives Cr(VI) reduction in deeper groundwater. We also show that the broader major element composition of the groundwater can be explained by equilibrium conditions with common ultramafic weathering minerals, in concert with this dissimilatory iron reduction. Furthermore, we demonstrate that, during our sampling, there is little-to-no dilution of mine-tailing wastewater with rainwater before discharge to surface waters (e.g. streams) within the valley, resulting in Cr(VI) contamination of these waters. We suggest that seasonal variations in rainfall may mitigate acute contamination during monsoon periods through dilution. We conclude that the deeper, reducing groundwater tapped by recently dug pump wells in the region effectively mitigates previously identified chromium contamination of drinking water in Sukinda but that surface waters remain impacted by direct runoff from mine-tailing sites. We suggest that enhanced dissimilatory iron reduction, through addition of organic matter, could be a feasible strategy for mitigating surface Cr(VI) contamination.

title: Environmental impact assessment of seal water systems during construction of rock cavern tanks at the Namikata National LPG stockpiling base: Characterization of scale deposition using scale surveys and column flow tests
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 205 Author(s): SeungYoul Yoo, Akira Ueda, Akiko Ozawa, Yasushi Kusakabe, Minenari Hiroki, Masahiro Ohkawa, Shinichi Tanikawa
abstract: Maintaining the groundwater level is crucial to prevent gas leaks from storage tanks during the construction and operation of underground liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) storage facilities. At the Namikata National LPG stockpiling base in Ehime Prefecture, Japan, deionized seawater is continuously injected into the subsurface as part of a seal water system. This process introduces mixing between injected water, groundwater, and seawater with varying chemical compositions, potentially leading to supersaturation of dissolved components and subsequent mineral precipitation within fractures, which may reduce the permeability of surrounding geological formations. Once a fracture becomes clogged, the groundwater flow pattern changes, and there is a risk that gases will move to shallower areas. In this study, the properties of precipitates (scales) formed in tunnel spring water at an underground LPG storage facility under construction were investigated to assess their implications for groundwater flow sustainability. The analyses included measurements of precipitation rates of calcium carbonate calcite preparations, bacterial surveys, and column flow tests simulating geological conditions to evaluate changes in permeability of tunnel spring water and seal water. The results showed that scales consisted of calcium carbonate, Mn oxides, and Fe oxides. Column flow tests using seal water demonstrated reduced water flow rates caused by Fe oxide precipitation, mainly associated with Fe rust released from pipe corrosion. By applying a geochemical clogging model to these flow rate reductions, we clarified the relationship between iron concentration in seal water and changes in permeability, and were able to propose measures such as replacing piping materials, thereby contributing to clogging prevention.

title: Polyphase of uranium mineralization in granite-related deposits: Insights from the geochronology and geochemistry of pitchblende and coffinite in the Xiwang uranium deposit, South China
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 205 Author(s): Bin Liu, Weifeng Chen, Haidong Li, Jiaming Qi, Liang Qiu, Hongfei Ling
abstract: Understanding the mechanisms of uranium enrichment, fluid evolution, and controls of multistage tectonic-magmatic activities in granite-related hydrothermal vein type uranium deposits remains a critical challenge. The Xiazhuang uranium ore-field, located in the southern section of the Taoshan-Zhuguang uranium metallogenic belt, is an important component of granite-related vein type uranium deposits in South China and serves as a natural laboratory for studying the metallogenic ages and processes of uranium mineralization. In this study, the most representative Xiwang uranium deposit is selected as the research target, and in situ microanalyses (using an electron probe micro-analyzer (EPMA) and laser ablation inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (LA-ICP-MS)) are carried out on mineralogy, geochronology, and elemental geochemistry of the uranium minerals—pitchblende and coffinite. The results show that each uranium mineral occurs in two morphological types: pitchblende appears as fine veins and spherulites, while coffinite occurs as fine veins and irregular granular forms. Their formation ages are 76.0 ± 2.8 Ma (n = 30, MSWD = 2.7) for the fine vein pitchblende, 53.9 ± 3.6 Ma (n = 22, MSWD = 0.76) for the spherulite pitchblende, and 19.0 ± 0.7 Ma (n = 7, MSWD = 2.1) for the fine vein coffinite. These ages indicate three stages of uranium mineralization (Late Cretaceous, Eocene, and Miocene). The total rare earth element (REE) contents in the fine vein and spherulite pitchblende range between 293 and 3721 ppm, with W concentrations of 6128 ∼ 10267 ppm, and nearly no Th, suggesting a medium-to-low temperature hydrothermal origin. The ores are enriched in U, W and other elements, and the REE distribution in pitchblende matches that of the host granitoids (Xiazhuang and Maofeng plutons), indicating that the ore-forming materials originated from these granitoids. Compared with the fine vein pitchblende, the spherulite pitchblende contains more W and Ca but less U, implying formation under a relatively more oxidizing environment. The fine vein and irregular granular coffinite in the Xiwang deposit formed differently: the former crystallized directly from U- and Si-bearing fluids, while the latter represents altered pre-existing pitchblende.

title: Geochemical modeling of CO 2 sequestration via weathering of steel slag: Reactive transport and mineralization dynamics
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 205 Author(s): E. Cosgun, J. Campbell, A. McBride, P. Wade, M. Van der Spek, P. Renforth
abstract: Carbon mineralization using steel slag represents a promising pathway for permanent CO2 storage; however, the coupled effects of reaction kinetics and transport processes under flow-through conditions remain incompletely constrained. This study evaluates the mechanistic controls and CO2 removal efficiency of percolation-driven carbonation using one-dimensional reactive transport modelling in PHREEQC. Simulations were performed for a 1 m-tall, packed column (1 m3 bulk steel slag volume), where infiltrating water equilibrated with CO2 mixtures (0.1-99 vol%) reacts with larnite-, portlandite-, periclase-, and brucite-bearing phases, promoting alkalinity generation and calcite precipitation. Model results identify three carbonation regimes. At ≤1 vol% CO2, carbonation is CO2-limited, resulting in shallow reaction fronts and low uptake (≤0.3 t CO2 per m3 of steel slag after 500 days). At ≥6 vol% CO2, rapid near-surface precipitation induces pore-scale passivation and transport limitation, restricting reaction progress despite high initial rates. Between these end-members, an optimal regime at ∼3-5 vol% CO2 enables coupled reaction-transport behaviour, sustaining Ca release and promoting deeper carbonation fronts (∼0.5-0.8 m). Under these conditions (∼4 vol% CO2), cumulative CO2 uptake reaches ∼0.56-0.60 t CO2 per m3 of steel slag (bulk volume basis) after one year, increasing to ∼0.68-0.71 t CO2 per m3 after 500 days. These values correspond to ∼0.30-0.33 and ∼0.37-0.39 t CO2 per tonne of slag, respectively, assuming a bulk density of 1.85 t m−3. Higher CO2 concentrations (99 vol%) yield greater initial uptake (∼0.94-1.01 t CO2 per m3), but with diminished long-term efficiency due to transport constraints. Extrapolation to Türkiye's projected 2025 steel slag production (4.6-5.7 Mt yr−1) indicates a theoretical CO2 removal potential of ∼1.4-2.2 Mt CO2 yr−1 under optimal conditions. These estimates represent upper bounds and are subject to limitations associated with reaction kinetics, fluid flow, and operational variability. The results provide quantitative constraints on process performance and highlight the importance of balancing reaction and transport processes for effective implementation of slag-based carbon mineralization.

title: Trace metal release induced by chemo-lithotrophic denitrification in deeper aquifers of the Lower Rhine Embayment, Germany
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 205 Author(s): Felix Fahrenbach, Thomas R. Rüde, Leonard Stoeckl, Georg J. Houben, Sarah E. Wünsch, Sven Sindern
abstract: Chemo-lithotrophic denitrification is a crucial process that mitigates high nitrate fluxes in suboxic aquifers; however, it bears the risk of increasing sulfate and trace metal concentrations, which are generally attributed to the pyrite oxidation involved. To assess trace metal release induced by this reaction, we link mineralogical-geochemical analyses to hydrochemical data. As an example, we investigate an area in the Lower Rhine Embayment, a Cenozoic sedimentary basin that hosts important groundwater resources in Western Germany. Geochemical analysis reveals that pyrite in the sediments contains arsenic, cobalt, copper, nickel, and zinc. The trace metals show a highly heterogeneous distribution between pyrite grains but also within individual pyrites. Analysis of groundwater samples indicates that chemo-lithotrophic denitrification results in the release of the aforementioned elements, except for copper. Subsequent oxidation and precipitation of a large proportion of the released iron produces protons, which are partly buffered by carbonate dissolution. Carbonate dissolution may be an additional trace metals source, especially for zinc. At the same time, precipitated iron(oxyhydr)oxides act as a sink for trace metals, particularly arsenic. The study demonstrates that trace metal release induced by chemo-lithotrophic denitrification depends on the trace metal content of pyrites, the extent of pyrite oxidation, the abundance and composition of additional mineral phases (e.g., carbonates), and the sorption and cation exchange capacity of the aquifer sediment.

title: Monitoring produced waters and groundwaters using strontium isotopes ( 87 Sr/ 86 Sr) at a CO 2 -enhanced oil recovery site in the Permian Basin
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 205 Author(s): James Gardiner, Rosemary Capo, Brian Stewart, Thai T. Phan, R. Burt Thomas, Mengling Stuckman, Christina Lopano, J. Alexandra Hakala
abstract: Monitoring injected carbon dioxide (CO2) during enhanced oil recovery (EOR) operations requires tools that demonstrate there is no fluid migration outside the target formation. Naturally occurring isotopes have the potential to indicate this type of fluid migration and identify geochemical reactions within the formation. This study provides a unique dataset of strontium isotope ratios (87Sr/86Sr) for produced waters and groundwaters prior to and during CO2 injection at a Permian Basin oil field. 87Sr/86Sr measurements over three years indicated no significant new sources of strontium were introduced within the target formation following CO2 injection. Produced waters from the Permian San Andres dolomite have distinctly higher Sr concentrations (19.1-38.5 mg L−1) and lower 87Sr/86Sr ratios (0.707882- 0.707961) compared with groundwater from the overlying Triassic Santa Rosa aquifer (0.293-0.825 mg L−1; 0.708391-0.708438) and Tertiary Ogallala aquifer (0.94-6.77 mg L−1; 0.708607-0.708682). Strontium isotope mixing models demonstrate that 87Sr/86Sr would be a sensitive tracer of formation water migration caused by CO2 injection. This study also demonstrates that the San Andres Fm. has lower 87Sr/86Sr than other proximal producing formations, suggesting that 87Sr/86Sr could be applied as a robust monitoring tool at regional CO2 injection sites.

title: Silica enrichment in a low-temperature granite aquifer: Supersaturation in weathering crust vs. enhanced dissolution in deep fractures
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 205 Author(s): Xiaoyan Zhang, Xumei Mao
abstract: Groundwater with elevated silica concentrations is rarely generated under natural conditions within silicate-dominated aquifers and has thus been relatively understudied. In the granite fracture network of Suining, South China, however, silica-enriched groundwater with low total dissolved solids (TDS) is notably abundant. Both the warm groundwater from the fractured granite (with dissolved silica concentrations up to 51.57 mg/L) and the shallow groundwater in the weathered granite zone (dissolved silica around 33.33 mg/L) display comparable hydrochemical characteristics. Hydrogeological and isotopic data (δD and δ18O) indicate an average recharge elevation of 613 m and a lateral recharge distance of approximately 3900 m from the Zishui-Yuanshui basin. Reservoir temperatures, estimated using the SiO2 geothermometer, vary between 66.5 °C and 74.6 °C, indicating a low-temperature geothermal system. Based on groundwater 14C ages (3.64–3.98 ka) and an inferred circulation depth of 3.09 km, the horizontal and vertical flow velocities are calculated to be approximately 2.8 × 10−3 m/d and 4.4 × 10−3 m/d, respectively. The conceptual hydrogeological model attributes silica enrichment to supersaturation of dissolved silica in surficial weathered granite and intensified silicate dissolution along deep fractures driven by elevated temperatures. Nevertheless, silica precipitation during groundwater ascent may lead to an underestimation of subsurface temperatures when the SiO2 geothermometer is applied in such low-temperature geothermal environments. Therefore, correctly evaluating the evolution process and genesis of dissolved silica within granite fracture networks is crucial for advancing the development and utilization of geothermal resources.

title: 7 Be, 210 Pb and 137 Cs in snow deposits on the territory of Altai krai, Novosibirsk and Tomsk oblasts
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 205 Author(s): Kseniya A. Mezina, Mikhail S. Melgunov, Dmitriy K. Belyanin
abstract: Radionuclides 7Be and 210Pb are widely used as tracers of atmospheric transport and deposition processes. This study investigates their deposition fluxes and distribution among different fractions of suspended and dissolved matter in snow water collected during the winter period 2020–2021 in the southern part of Western Siberia. The mean deposition fluxes of 7Be and 210Pb were 94 ± 57 and 48 ± 26 Bq/m2, respectively, over a five-month period of stable snow accumulation. 137Cs exhibited negligible values ( 3 μm), whereas 7Be is mainly concentrated in finely dispersed aerosols, colloids, and a dissolved component (<0.45 μm), reflecting differences in their origin and atmospheric residence time. A clear spatial differentiation of sampling sites into two groups was identified. In areas with increased anthropogenic load, a significant shift of 7Be toward coarse-grained fractions was observed, accompanied by strong correlations between 7Be and 210Pb in these fractions. In contrast, conditionally background sites exhibited stronger relationships in the finely fraction. These results indicate that anthropogenic activity affects not only the total radionuclide content but also their distribution among particle size fractions. The observed patterns reflect differences in aerosol sources, transport pathways, and deposition mechanisms, highlighting the importance of particle size and environmental conditions in controlling radionuclide behavior in snow cover.

title: Zinc isotope fractionation during the interaction with different molecular weight fractions of dissolved organic matter
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 205 Author(s): Qiyuan Liu, Yaqin Zhang, Zening Lü, Tongying Yan, Rui Zuo, Yuanzheng Zhai, Liuting Song
abstract: The bioavailability and mobility of zinc (Zn) are predominantly governed by dissolved organic matter (DOM) in natural environments. Although Zn isotopes are known to fractionate during complexation with organic ligands, the mechanism of how DOM heterogeneity modulates this process remains poorly constrained. In this study, we investigated Zn isotope fractionation induced by complexation with different molecular weight (MW) fractions of two natural DOM: Pahokee Peat Fulvic Acid (PPFA) and Suwannee River Fulvic Acid (SRFA). The Donnan Membrane Technique (DMT) was employed to separate Zn-DOM complexes from free Zn species. The results indicate that while no discernible isotopic fractionation was observed ( Δ 66 Z n C o m p l e x − F r e e = −0.12‰ to +0.06‰) induced by bulk PPFA and SRFA, the MW-fractionated components displayed a broad range of distinct isotopic fractionation ( Δ 66 Z n C o m p l e x − F r e e = −0.01‰ to +0.55‰). For PPFA fractions, heavy Zn isotopes are preferentially enriched in the Zn complexes ( Δ 66 Z n C o m p l e x − F r e e = +0.28‰ to +0.30‰), which is attributed to the formation of strong, stable bonds with abundant aromatic phenolic moieties, particularly within the high-MW fractions. SRFA components exhibited more pronounced isotopic fractionation compared to PPFA, with Δ 66 Z n values reaching up to +0.55‰ for the 100–1000 kDa fraction and +0.53‰ for the <10 kDa fraction. This enhanced fractionation is primarily attributed to the formation of stronger inner-sphere complexes with shorter Zn-ligand bond lengths, likely involving coordination with carboxyl and/or hydroxyl functional groups. This study reveals how structural and functional group differences among different MW fractions of DOM affect metal complexation capacity and consequently influence Zn isotope fractionation, providing a better understanding of Zn biogeochemical cycling in natural systems.

title: Defining pedo-geochemical backgrounds in former mining area by reinforcing the soil sampling strategies and advanced geostatistical approaches
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 205 Author(s): Jérémie Melleton, Stéphane Belbeze, Philippe Négrel, Guillaume Vic, Pascal Auger, Matthieu Chevillard, Ingrid Girardeau, Dominique Guyonnet, Florence Rivet
abstract: Evaluation of the impacts of former mining activities on soil quality requires the determination of pedo-geochemical backgrounds for potentially toxic elements such as arsenic. Difficulties in such a context may arise from high geogenic concentrations related to the presence of mineralization in the mined area. In this study, we investigated the pedo-geochemical background in the former Au–As Salsigne mining district located in the South of the French Massif Central. Sampling of topsoils was designed such as to discard sites with evident influence of mining activities and with the aim to obtain a sufficient amount of data to be able to determine representative statistical parameters. A suitable number of sampling sites (150) was obtained by grouping existing litho-tectonic units into three coherent geological domains: the Axial zone domain, the Minervois nappes domain and the Cenozoic domain. For some of the investigated elements such as arsenic, the distribution of soil concentrations shows areas with higher pedo-geochemical background close to mineralization. Advanced statistical methods such as Minimum-Maximum Autocorrelation Factors (MAFs) allow a distinction of such enriched zones in order to better estimate pedo-geochemical background values. The proposed methodology for determining pedogeochemical backgrounds is applicable in other areas that display complex geology with significant natural variations of soil concentrations such as in mineralized areas where mining activities may have occurred.

title: Dissolution kinetics of steel slag in ammonium chloride solutions for carbon mineralization: An experimental study and implications for carbon capture and sequestration
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 205 Author(s): Fan Liu, Liang Zhao, Chen Zhu, Gen K. Li
abstract: Steel slag – the solid waste generated from steelmaking – has fine particle sizes and contains abundant alkaline metals (e.g., Ca), making it a promising material for carbonation, a process that sequesters carbon dioxide (CO2) as carbonates. The carbonation capacity of steel slag depends heavily on the solution used to leach alkaline ions (e.g., Ca2+) from slag. Previous studies have proposed ammonium chloride (NH4Cl) as an effective leaching solution for its efficient leaching of Ca2+, the production of economically valuable high-purity carbonates as byproducts, and its feasibility for recycling. However, the reaction kinetics of steel-slag-NH4Cl systems remain less well quantified. Here we present an experimental study of leaching steel slag in NH4Cl solutions for carbonation purposes. We tested a range of solvents and validated the efficacy of using steel slag and NH4Cl for carbonation. We then tested different reaction conditions for the steel-slag-NH4Cl system and identified that an NH4Cl solution concentration of 1-2 M and a solid-to-liquid ratio of 100-200 g/L could yield both high leaching efficiency and high selectivity for Ca2+. Lastly, we performed time-series leaching experiments to characterize the reaction kinetics. The results demonstrated that the steel-slag-NH4Cl system can be well described by a shrinking-core model and the reaction is limited by the diffusion of NH4Cl into slag particles. Extrapolating our findings, we estimate that slag-NH4Cl-based carbonation has the potential to sequester up to ∼9% of CO2 emission from steelmaking. Overall, our work characterizes the reaction kinetics of the steel-slag-NH4Cl system for carbonation, laying a solid foundation for developing strategies for industrial upscaling.

title: Fluoride as a tracer of vertical hydraulic connectivity in volcanic aquifers: Decadal hydrogeochemical response to seismic activity in Tenerife (Canary Islands)
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 205 Author(s): E. de Miguel-García, J.F. Gómez-González
abstract: Volcanic aquifers are highly sensitive to tectonic perturbations, which may modify groundwater circulation patterns and alter water–rock–gas interactions. In Tenerife (Canary Islands), a seismic event of magnitude 3.8 mbLg in 2012 was followed by a marked hydrogeochemical anomaly characterized by an increase in dissolved fluoride (F−) and a gradual decline during the subsequent years. This study investigates the mechanisms controlling this evolution through a combination of long-term hydrogeochemical monitoring (2011–2020), statistical analysis, and geochemical modelling using PHREEQC, including thermodynamic calculations, surface complexation modelling on iron oxyhydroxides, and mixing scenarios between groundwater end-members. Results show that fluoride concentrations increased from 0.034 mmol L−1 in 2012 to 0.061 mmol L−1 in 2014. This rise is quantitatively reproduced by conservative mixing between intermediate aquifer groundwater and a deep basal groundwater end-member, with an estimated basal contribution of approximately 18%. The subsequent fluoride decline between 2014 and 2020 is explained by progressive mixing with low-fluoride meteoric recharge waters (∼10% contribution per stage). Thermodynamic calculations indicate that groundwater remained strongly undersaturated with respect to fluorite throughout the study period, while surface complexation modelling shows that adsorption onto iron oxyhydroxides accounts for less than 5% of total fluoride removal. These results demonstrate that mixing processes dominate the hydrogeochemical response of the aquifer following the seismic perturbation. The study highlights the usefulness of fluoride as a tracer of vertical hydraulic connectivity in volcanic aquifers and provides a framework for interpreting post-seismic groundwater evolution in tectonically active volcanic regions.

title: Geo-engineering materials for simultaneous ammonium and phosphate control: binding capacity, desorption behavior and sediment nutrient release
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 205 Author(s): Yuxin Shi, Maíra Mucci, Miquel Lürling
abstract: Eutrophication is a growing concern in aquatic ecosystems. This study evaluated geo-engineering materials like natural zeolite (NZ), lanthanum-modified bentonite (LMB), aluminum-modified zeolite (AMZ), lanthanum-modified zeolite (LMZ), and selected combinations for nutrient removal using batch experiments and sediment cores. NZ only adsorbed NH4 + (4.86 mg N g−1) while LMB only removed soluble reactive phosphate (SRP) (11.70 mg P g−1). AMZ and LMZ removed both SRP and NH4 + (AMZ: 7.18 mg N g−1 and 8.22 mg P g−1; LMZ: 8.30 mg N g−1 and 8.60 mg P g−1). Combining NZ and LMB (0.05 or 0.1 g each) resulted in half the SRP adsorption capacity compared to LMB alone, while maintaining similar NH4 + adsorption capacity to NZ. AMZ and LMB combined showed similar SRP binding to AMZ, but lower NH4 + adsorption (2.54 and 2.87 mg N g−1). The interference of potassium ions strongly reduced the NH4 + adsorption capacity of NZ. LMZ released 1062 μg La g−1, over 50 times more than LMB, while AMZ released 0.45 mg Al g−1. NZ reduced the NH4 +-N sediment flux by 86% compared to the control, but did not affect the P flux. LMB reduced the phosphate flux by 80% compared to the control, but did not affect the N flux. AMZ and NZ + LMB reduced both the P (>80%) and N (>50%) fluxes. Considering availability, safety, and efficiency, AMZ and the NZ and LMB combination seem promising to manage both sediment N and P release and are well-suited for further upscaling experiments in lake restoration research.

title: Nitrogen contents and natural 15 N abundance of proteins in plants and soils: Analytical methods and biogeochemical implications
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 205 Author(s): Song-Hua Li, Xue-Yan Liu
abstract: Proteins are pivotal organic nitrogen (N) species. Producing, accumulating and consuming mechanisms of proteins are critical information for understanding the nature and role of organic N pools in terrestrial N biogeochemistry. N contents and natural 15N abundance (δ15N) of extractable proteins (EPN) can provide new insights into protein dynamics in plants and soils, whereas analytical methods of these parameters remain unestablished. Here we established a pretreating protocol for EPN in plants and soils and conducted a field investigation at the Mt. Dongling forest of western Beijing. We recommend the alkali dissolution (pH = 14) and acid precipitation (pH = 2–5) for extracting and purifying proteins from plant and soil samples. At the Mt. Dongling forest, leaf and soil EPN averaged 7.19 ± 0.20 and 0.15 ± 0.002 mg N g−1 dw, accounting for 56 ± 2% and 8 ± 0.2% in respective bulk N. The δ15N of EPN in leaves and soils averaged −3.0 ± 0.1‰ and 1.6 ± 0.2‰, differing from the respective bulk δ15N (−4.5 ± 0.1‰ and 1.9 ± 0.2‰). Further analyses revealed that leaf EPN is largely labile and its 15N enrichment relative to bulk N was attributed to the 15N discrimination during amino acid transamination. Differently, EPN is a small fraction in soil organic N pool, and their similar δ15N values reflected a marginal N fractionation in organic N decomposition. Our analytical methods and new insights into EPN provide a foundation for further exploration of protein dynamics in the ‘gray box’ of organic N biogeochemistry under global changes.

title: Evaluation of geochemical changes in coastal aquifers induced by seawater intrusion and CO 2 leakage using column experiments
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 205 Author(s): Jisu Jeong, Hyun-Kwon Do, Soyeon Lim, Hakyung Cho, Sung-Wook Jeen
abstract: Understanding the hydrogeochemical impacts of seawater intrusion and CO2 leakage is critical for assessing the stability of coastal aquifers near offshore carbon storage sites. This study investigated the coupled effects of these two perturbations through laboratory column experiments using two representative media—Quaternary alluvial soil (QA) and crushed basalt (CB)—common in Korean coastal aquifers and potential CO2 storage formations. Each column underwent four experimental phases: saturation with synthetic groundwater (SGW), injection of 10% artificial seawater (ASW), injection of CO2-saturated 10% ASW, and back-flushing with SGW. Temporal and spatial analyses of geochemical parameters, major cations, and trace elements were used to evaluate dominant reaction mechanisms and lithology-dependent responses. Seawater intrusion primarily induced cation exchange, especially in clay-rich QA, while CO2 leakage suppressed exchange reactions and promoted acid-enhanced mineral dissolution. CB exhibited stronger dissolution signals, with elevated concentrations of Mg, Si, and trace elements including Al and Fe. Secondary mineral precipitation—particularly of Al- and Fe-bearing phases—limited downstream transport under acidic conditions. During freshening, full geochemical recovery was not achieved due to immobile pore water in QA and relatively short retention time in CB. While both seawater intrusion and CO2 leakage increased solute concentrations, only CO2 leakage produced significant acidification and broad mineral dissolution. These findings highlight the importance of distinguishing geochemical signatures when designing CCS monitoring strategies. Geochemical parameters (e.g., pH, Si, Al, and Fe) may serve as diagnostic indicators of CO2 leakage in both QA and CB media. This study underscores the influence of sediment properties on geochemical responses and supports risk-informed monitoring at offshore carbon storage sites.

title: Isotopic fingerprints of CO 2 release from low-temperature oxidation of coal tailings using oxygen consumption experiments
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 205 Author(s): Abdulraheem O. Anumah, Suzanne D. Golding, Gordon Southam, Mansour Edraki
abstract: Oxidation of residual sulfides in mine tailings generates acid, which can dissolve carbonate minerals and release CO2. In coal tailings, CO2 may also be produced through the oxidation of abundant organic matter and bacterial respiration. The commonly used kinetic leaching and oxygen consumption experiments have not been designed to measure CO2; consequently, the role of CO2 concentrations in rate calculations remains poorly understood, and a potentially important source of greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions may be overlooked. This limitation may have implications for predicting the long-term chemical stability of coal tailings storage facilities and, therefore, for mine closure and rehabilitation planning. This study investigated the isotopic composition of CO2 generated during low-temperature oxidation of coal tailings to identify the relative contributions of organic and inorganic carbon sources. Oxygen consumption experiments were performed under controlled moisture, microbial, particle size and mineralogical conditions, followed by gas-chromatographic and isotope-ratio mass spectrometry analyses of CO2, CH4, and O2. The δ13C-CO2 and δ18O-CO2 values ranged from -19.9‰ to +3.6‰ (VPDB) and from +30.6‰ to +44.7‰ (VSMOW), respectively, reflecting strong isotopic differentiation across hydrological and biogeochemical regimes. Moisture availability exerted the primary control on both CO2 yield and isotopic enrichment, while inoculation with mixed acidophilic bacterial cultures accelerated sulfide oxidation but did not significantly alter isotopic signatures. Dry samples at 0% gravimetric water content (GWC) released CO2 with isotopically depleted δ13C and δ18O values consistent with organic carbon oxidation. In contrast, moist samples (10% GWC) under acid-promoted conditions produced isotopically enriched CO2 indicative of carbonate dissolution and microbial catalysis. These results demonstrate that δ13C-δ18O systematics provide a reliable diagnostic framework for distinguishing organic-from carbonate-derived CO2 emissions in coal mine tailings, with broader applicability to other sulfide-bearing mine wastes. The findings highlight the benefit of incorporating isotopic tracing into mine-waste kinetic assessments to better inform closure and rehabilitation strategies and support quantification of potential greenhouse gas emissions from this under-reported source.

title: Direct evidence for enhanced mineral weathering in cropland verified by quantitative X-ray powder diffraction
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 205 Author(s): Kohei Kurokawa, Atsushi Nakao, Kazuki Azuma, Hodaka Tomita, Katashi Kubo, Kazuki Nomura, Junta Yanai
abstract: Enhanced rock weathering (ERW) is a promising carbon dioxide (CO2) removal (CDR) strategy that involves applying powdered rocks such as basalt to croplands to accelerate the natural weathering of rock minerals. However, despite numerous recent field investigations, direct evidence for the weathering of rock minerals in soils is lacking because most studies rely on cation budgets to estimate ERW-induced CDR. In this study, buckwheat was cultivated for 2.5 months in plots with and without basalt powder applied at a rate of 150 t ha−1, and the decrease in basaltic mineral contents of the soils during the cultivation period was measured using quantitative X-ray powder diffraction (XRPD). Applying basalt powder significantly increased the contents of basaltic minerals such as plagioclase (e.g., labradorite and bytownite) and pyroxene in the soils, and the basaltic mineral contents subsequently decreased significantly in the rootzone after cultivation. The decrease was about 8.5 times greater in the rootzone than outside the rootzone. The percentage decrease relative to the input in the rootzone was 25.6% for labradorite, 58.8% for bytownite, and 65.1% for pyroxene, reflecting the theoretical dissolution mass and the more rapid weathering of bytownite and pyroxene compared to labradorite. The maximum CDR associated with the weathering of these minerals was estimated as 7.2 t CO2 ha−1 over 2.5 months. These results provide the first quantitative evidence for the weathering of basaltic minerals applied to cropland and demonstrate the feasibility of applying state-of-the-art XRPD analysis to the monitoring, reporting, and verification of ERW-induced CDR under field conditions.

title: Subsurface chlorophyll maximum plays a critical role in water column primary productivity in a large reservoir: evidence from high-resolution diel O 2 mass balance
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 205 Author(s): Yongsheng Chu, Xiaoying Li, Xueping Chen, Shengman Zhang, Ruifang Wang, Haocheng Miao, Fushun Wang
abstract: Phytoplankton are essential to aquatic primary productivity and carbon cycling. Subsurface chlorophyll-a maximum (SCM) layer often forms hotspots of primary productivity. Its complex spatiotemporal dynamics hinder accurate quantification of its contribution to water column gross primary productivity (GPP) and carbon fixation using conventional periodic sampling. This study focused on Xin'anjiang Reservoir, integrating high-frequency monitoring data (2019–2021) with a diel oxygen model. We estimated high-resolution GPP synchronized with SCM dynamics and examined the environmental regulators of SCM, and its contribution patterns to GPP. Results showed strong spatiotemporal heterogeneity in SCM. SCM occurred mainly during stratified periods, but not continuously, and were easily disrupted by rainfall and wind. Mean GPP was 350 ± 139 mg C m−2 d−1 during 2019–2021. Annually, SCM contributed 21–38% of whole-reservoir water column GPP, increasing to 66–77% of local water column GPP in the dam zone during summer. SCM was regulated by thermal stratification and euphotic zone depth. Water level indirectly influenced GPP via effects on thermal stratification and SCM characteristics. These findings elucidate the critical role of SCM in reservoir carbon cycling and the regulatory potential of water level management, providing a scientific basis for reservoir ecological management and carbon budget assessments.

title: Silicate-bound 3-hydroxy fatty acids in marine sediments: temperature signals and implications
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 205 Author(s): Zhongyuan Luo, Guodong Jia
abstract: Mineral-bound (MB) organic matter constitutes a large yet under-utilized sedimentary archive of molecular fossils. Here, we liberate silicate-bound (SB) 3-hydroxy fatty acids (3-OH-FAs) by hydrofluoric acid (HF) digestion from surface sediments of the East China Sea (ECS) and South China Sea (SCS) and evaluate their palaeothermometric potential relative to conventionally obtained non-SB (NSB) counterparts. SB-3-OH-FAs account for 61–94% of the total 3-OH-FA inventory and are preferentially enriched in short-chain (C10–C14) homologues. Among the established temperature indices derived from 3-OH-FAs, NSB-derived RAN13 correlates with sea surface temperature in both the ECS and SCS. However, the SB-derived RAN13-SB exhibits a water-column-specific response: in the shallow, moderately-mixed ECS, it correlates with the whole water-column mean temperature (R2 = 0.86), whereas in the deep, stratified SCS, it tracks intermediate water temperature at ∼325 m (R2 = 0.61). A mineral-microbe interaction model in the water column is proposed to explain the distinct temperature signals between NSB- and SB-3-OH-FAs in the SCS—the NSB-C13 3-OH-FAs potentially derive from surface phototrophic bacteria, while the SB-C13 3-OH-FAs originate from mesopelagic heterotrophic proteobacteria that replace the clay-mineral-associated counterparts during organic matter decomposition and bacterial community reorganization. The HF digestion method thus unlocks a previously inaccessible palaeoceanographic repository and redefines clay minerals as active agents in shaping depth-specific thermal signals rather than passive preservation matrices.

title: Sustainable River-Basin management under monsoon variability: Spatio-temporal hydrochemistry and water-quality suitability in the Kankai Basin of Nepal Himalaya
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 205 Author(s): Anuradha Dhakal, Moti Lal Rijal, Tista Prasai Joshi, Mahesh Prasad Awasthi, Gobinda Prasad Pokharel, Ahmed M. Saqr
abstract: River-water quality is deteriorating globally due to intensified land use, expanding wastewater inputs, and climate-driven hydrological variability that reshapes sediment and solute transport. This study investigates these challenges in the Himalayan Kankai River Basin in Nepal, which was selected because it is a monsoon-driven Himalayan–Terai River system with strong elevation contrasts and major irrigation dependence. The objectives were to characterize seasonal surface-water hydrochemistry, identify controlling mechanisms, map spatio-temporal hotspot behavior, assess drinking and irrigation suitability, and develop a Sustainable River-Basin Management Strategy (SRBMS). Surface-water chemistry was evaluated from 76 samples (38 pre-monsoon and 38 post-monsoon) using field and laboratory analyses of physicochemical variables and major ions. These analyses were supported by Geographic Information System (GIS) mapping, multivariate statistics, and hydrochemical diagrams. Water was slightly alkaline (pH 6.3–8.9 pre-monsoon; 6.7–9.0 post-monsoon), and dissolved oxygen was low (1.9–4.6 and 2.3–4.5 mg/L). Turbidity peaks increased after the monsoon (144.74 to 319.66 NTU), and ammonium maxima rose from 23.59 to 39.76 mg/L, indicating stronger post-monsoon stress in hotspot areas. Ca–Mg–HCO3 facies dominated (72.3% pre-monsoon; 56.3% post-monsoon), while Gibbs plots showed rock-weathering control. Water Quality Index (WQI) was predominantly unsuitable (76.31% of pre- and 86.84% of post-monsoon samples) for drinking. Irrigation screening indicated low sodium hazard with excellent Sodium Adsorption Ratio (SAR) values, but magnesium hazard (MH) was frequently unsuitable. The proposed SRBMS and the integrated workflow provide actionable, season-aware evidence applicable to other monsoon-affected mountain plain basins facing similar conditions worldwide.

title: Elucidating the origin of sulphate in the Upper Silesian Coal Basin in southern Poland using machine learning clustering and Bayesian mixing model
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 205 Author(s): Katarzyna Samborska-Goik, Ondra Sracek
abstract: The Upper Silesian Coal Basin (USCB) is one of the largest and most productive coal basins in Europe. The basin's geological structure, together with its extensive network of shafts and underground galleries, has given rise to a highly complex hydrological system. This study employs machine-learning clustering and Bayesian modelling, combined with isotopic analyses of dissolved sulphate in mine water, to identify the principal sources of sulphate. Geological interpretation further validates the clustering results, reinforcing the underlying conceptual framework. The results indicate that sulphate in the investigated mines originates from three isotopically distinct sources: (1) oxidation of sulphidic minerals and organic matter, (2) dissolution of Badenian evaporites, characterised by narrow ranges of δ34S and δ18O values, and (3) inflow of highly mineralized brines from deeper formations, for which the sulphate isotopic signatures suggest an Early Triassic origin. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study in which a clustering model based solely on isotopic data has been applied to identify sulphate sources in mine waters and subsequently validated using independent chemical and geological evidence. Furthermore, this work is novel in combining clustering output (cluster centroids) with a Bayesian isotope mixing model in order to assess within-cluster homogeneity and quantify mixing processes and their relative contributions. These findings demonstrate that clustering methods provide robust insight into hydrogeochemical systems and are particularly valuable where comprehensive chemical data are unavailable or limited. Moreover, mine waters are increasingly recognized as a potential resource for potable and industrial use rather than merely as waste. Consequently, studies addressing their origin, evolution and quality are essential for evaluating future water-supply opportunities and supporting sustainable water-management strategies, including the identification of locations with potential for potable water abstraction.

title: Characterizing nickel adsorption-desorption on kaolinite
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 205 Author(s): Soumya Das, M. Jim Hendry, Peter E.R. Blanchard
abstract: The pH dependent (∼2-11) adsorption-desorption behavior of nickel (Ni2+) on kaolinite was characterized in two experiments in deionized (DI; I = 0.005 M) water and a higher ionic strength coal mine drainage water (I = ∼0.1 M). In the adsorption (using NaOH) phases of all experiments, ∼10 mg/L Ni2+ spikes were completely removed by pH ∼8.8-9.7. In the two (1 d and 3 d long) adsorption experiments conducted in DI water, 29-36% of the spiked Ni2+ was adsorbed at the onset of testing (pH ∼2.3) consistent with adsorption to permanent structurally charged sites (outer sphere complexation). The sorption edges became sharper at pH ∼6.7-6.8 (the inflection point) where ∼45-53% of the spiked Ni2+ was adsorbed consistent with the activation of variable charged edge sites (inner sphere complexation). At the end of the desorption (using HCl) phase of the DI water experiments (pH∼2.0-2.2), ∼31-55% of the adsorbed Ni2+ has desorbed. Lower concentrations of the desorbed Ni2+ (∼31%) in the 3 d vs the 1 d experiments in DI water (∼55%) at pH ∼2.0-2.2 suggest increasing reaction/residence time increases Ni2+ stability on kaolinite surfaces. In contrast to the DI water experiments, a decrease in adsorption was observed during the adsorption phase of the mine drainage water experiment. For example, in the desorption phase, most (∼95%) of the adsorbed Ni2+ was desorbed at pH ∼2.1. EXAFS spectra suggest Ni2+ adsorption to both basal mineral surfaces and variable edge sites. The first coordination shell spectra (∼1.65 Å) correspond to a Ni–O scattering path, likely to basal mineral surfaces, whereby the Ni atoms are in an octahedral coordination environment irrespective of pH. The second coordination shell spectra (∼2.7 Å) correspond to Ni–Al/Si/Ni scattering paths reflecting Ni2+ adsorption on mineral edged as a NiO6 octahedra bond which increase in intensity with increasing pH. A single Ni–Ni scattering path was also observed at pHs greater than ∼7.2, possibly indicating the formation of NiO6 octahedra clusters on the kaolinite surface.

title: Use of radiocarbon and stable carbon isotope for evaluating the provenance and cycling of particulate organic carbon in a hyper-eutrophic lake, China
description: Publication date: July 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 204 Author(s): Tao Zhang, Haiquan Yang, Jingan Chen, Jingfu Wang, Yilong Song, Qinlin Wang, Xuyin Tang, Shuwen Sun
abstract: Particulate organic carbon (POC) is a key component of carbon and energy flow in lacustrine ecosystems, yet its sources and cycling remain poorly quantified in hyper-eutrophic lakes. This study applied a dual-isotope (Δ14C-δ13C) approach combined with SIAR to quantify the spatiotemporal dynamics and sources of POC in hyper-eutrophic Lake Dianchi. Results showed a substantial POC stock of approximately 3.24 × 109 g C in the lake, exhibiting marked seasonal and spatial variations driven by algal primary production, terrestrial inputs, and sediment resuspension. During summer, POC concentrations were higher in the north and lower in the south, influenced by prevailing winds; this spatial pattern reversed in winter due to enhanced vertical mixing and increased terrestrial inputs. SIAR modeling indicates that algal production dominates the POC pool (71.4 ± 5.4%), followed by terrestrial inputs (13.9 ± 5.7%) and resuspended sediment-derived POC (14.7 ± 2.3%). Dual-isotope evidence further showed a substantial contribution of aged organic carbon derived from the watershed, contrasting with the internal sedimentary recycling processes commonly observed in deeper, less productive lakes. These findings highlight fundamentally different carbon cycling pathways in shallow, eutrophic systems compared to stratified oligotrophic lakes. Overall, the dual-isotope framework presented here offers a robust tool for clarifying POC transformation under eutrophic conditions and provides a scientific basis for managing nutrient sources and mitigating internal loading in Lake Dianchi and other eutrophic lakes.

title: The vertical distribution and redox-dependent mobilization of arsenic in naturally contaminated karstic paddy soils from southwestern China
description: Publication date: July 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 204 Author(s): Qi Gao, Manman Zhao, Ying Wang, Hang Li, Zengping Ning, Jing Sun, Chengshuai Liu, Yizhang Liu
abstract: Soil arsenic (As) contamination is a global environmental issue, and geogenic enrichment of As in soils derived from carbonate rocks is of increasing concern. However, the geochemical partitioning and biogeochemical processes of As in paddy soils in carbonate regions remain poorly understood. In this study, four paddy soil profiles were collected from a typical karst area in southwestern China to investigate the distribution, speciation, and bioavailability of As. A composite surface paddy soil sample was also collected for microcosm incubation to elucidate As behavior under redox alternation. The results showed that the As content in the soils ranged from 28.48 to 74.21 mg/kg, exceeding the risk screening value for agricultural land. Vertically, As was uniformly distributed across the soil profiles. On average, approximately 81% of As was bound to crystalline Fe oxides, while the proportion of mobile fractions was low. Additionally, the proportion of bioavailable As extracted with 0.43 M HNO3 ranged from 0.56% to 2.57% (mean = 1.08%), with higher values observed in surface layers than in deeper layers. Correlation analysis revealed that the bioavailable fraction of As was positively correlated with soil organic matter content. Soil reduction-oxidation microcosm incubation revealed that aqueous As concentrations gradually increased during the anoxic period, plateaued from day 31 to 40, and then rapidly decreased during the subsequent oxic period. The synchronous variation in aqueous As and Fe(II) concentrations suggests that Fe oxide transformation plays a key role in governing As behavior under redox alternation in these naturally As-rich paddy soils. These results highlight the potential risks of As in paddy soils during flooding conditions, even if its immediate bioavailability is low. Our findings provide guidelines for managing As pollution in paddy soils in karst areas with a high geologic background.

title: Influence of inundation frequency on soil organic carbon stability in northern China's estuarine wetlands
description: Publication date: July 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 204 Author(s): Zhanhang Liu, Hu Ding, Xiaokun Han, Hao Xue, Chunmei Chen, Cong-qiang Liu, Yunchao Lang
abstract: Estuarine intertidal wetlands are significant blue carbon sinks, yet the mechanisms by which inundation frequency affects soil organic carbon (SOC) stability remain unclear in bare flat. This study investigated the effects of inundation frequency (14%–78%), seasonal variation, and soil depth on SOC fractions in intertidal wetlands of the Liao River Estuary, northern China. SOC stability was evaluated by the ratio of mineral-associated organic carbon (MAOC) to particulate organic carbon (POC), which reflects the overall stability of the carbon pool by quantifying the proportion stabilized through mineral association. In summer, microbial biomass carbon (MBC) was higher than in winter (32.0 vs. 14.3 mg kg −1) and POC also increased significantly, whereas MAOC remained unchanged, showing a seasonal decoupling between fast-cycling and slower-cycling carbon fractions. Structural equation modeling (SEM) confirmed a significant, direct negative effect of inundation frequency on MAOC. Our findings reveal a decoupling between the accumulation pathways of POC and MAOC. The microbial biomass nitrogen (MBN) is identified as the primary predictor for POC, while clay content was the most important predictor for MAOC. Linear relationships suggest that the MAOC content is sustained through alternative pathways rather than the direct transformation of local POC. Results indicate that in estuarine intertidal wetlands, the enrichment of fine mineral particles (clay) driven by hydrodynamic sorting dominates the formation of MAOC, rather than the accumulation of POC from plant inputs. These findings highlight the regulatory role of inundation frequency in SOC preservation and blue carbon persistence in estuarine systems.

title: Hydrothermal mobilization of heavy rare earth elements in carbonate-rich systems: Implications from the Arıklı mineralization (NW Türkiye)
description: Publication date: July 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 204 Author(s): Gokhan Buyukkahraman
abstract: The mobilization and enrichment of heavy rare earth elements (HREE) in carbonate-hosted hydrothermal systems remain poorly constrained due to limited thermodynamic and experimental data. This study re-evaluates the Arıklı Th–U–HREE mineralization in northwestern Türkiye to explore the geochemical plausibility of late-stage fluid–rock interaction and ligand-controlled speciation processes in carbonate-bearing environments. Modeling of solubility trends suggests that moderate-temperature (120–180 °C), moderately alkaline (pH 10–11) fluids may facilitate the transport of HREE via carbonate–hydroxyl complexation. These inferred conditions are consistent with recent experimental and thermodynamic studies, indicating that late-stage HREE redistribution could occur without the direct involvement of high-temperature magmatic fluids. The findings highlight the importance of fluid chemistry and ligand availability in potentially modifying REE fractionation during post-orogenic hydrothermal alteration.

title: Supergene enrichment-dominated gold mineralization in the Phayaung Taung deposit, Myanmar
description: Publication date: July 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 204 Author(s): Naing Aung Khant, Cheolhong Kim, Heejung Kim, Khin Zaw, Dongbok Shin, Yeongmin Kim, Joowan Kim, Chungwan Lim
abstract: The Phayaung Taung gold deposit is situated within the Late Proterozoic Chaung Magyi Group, located in the southern segment of the Mogok Metamorphic Belt (MMB), also recognized as the Mergui Belt (MB). The fluid inclusion data indicates that the deposit is from an orogenic origin with the salinity range of 3.4 wt% to 12.9 wt% NaCl equivalent and the homogenization temperature of 218.0 °C to 450.0 °C for the bi-phase liquid-rich fluid inclusions. And it shows local upgrading of gold mineralization by supergene enrichment processes in which gold occurs with the secondary sulfide minerals, such as digenite, djurleite, stromeyerite, covellite, etc. Gold initially precipitated during hypogene mineralization within the orogenic system was subsequently remobilized in acidic aqueous solutions, formed by the oxidation of primary sulfide minerals by meteoric water. Gold occurs in the quartzite and phyllite units but major mineralization is concentrated within the quartzite units, owing to the inherently brittle nature of quartzite. This brittleness enhances its susceptibility to fracturing, thereby facilitating the formation of conduits for ore-bearing fluids. Consequently, the lithological interface between quartzite and phyllite units represents a significant target for gold exploration. Primary copper sulfide minerals, such as chalcopyrite and bornite, have been economically upgraded to more copper-rich secondary sulfide minerals like covellite, digenite, and djurleite. Therefore, at the Phayaung Taung deposit, the recovery of copper should be strategically considered as a by-product alongside gold extraction. This comprehensive understanding of the deposit's characteristics and mineralization mechanisms is crucial for developing effective exploration strategies and evaluating economic viability.

title: Comparative evaluation of deep-penetrating geochemistry (DPG) for concealed Au deposit and exploration strategies in semi-arid central China
description: Publication date: July 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 204 Author(s): Yuying Huyan, Ke Yang, Zhenyu Ma, Yiwei Song, Wang Zhang, Zhanbin Wang, Wei Yang, Dongxiang Jiang, Yongbao Gao, Liyong Wei
abstract: The West Qinling Orogen (WQO) is a critical region for China's gold reserves. However, as exploration progresses, the search for exposed orebodies or shallow deposits has become increasingly challenging. Various overburden materials (e.g., loess, grassland, sedimentary rocks) obscure mineralization signals, leading to high exploration costs. To address this challenge, deep-penetrating geochemistry (DPG) methods, including soil gas geochemical surveys (SGGS), the fine-grained soil prospecting method (FGSPM), and leaching of mobile forms of metals in overburden (MOMEO), were performed at the Zhaishang concealed Au deposit in the semi-arid region to evaluate their applicability. The results showed that all three DPG methods correlated well with gold deposits and alteration zones beneath the loess cover. SGGS were the most sensitive, particularly for H2S and SO2, displaying extensive gas responses. In contrast, the FGSPM and MOMEO methods produced more stable but fewer geochemical peaks, with a sampling grain size of <75 μm. MOMEO was especially effective in enhancing weak Au signals from thin gold layers, with active Au primarily absorbed in clay minerals and organic matter (e.g., nanoparticles). However, the spatial locations of geochemical anomalies varied among the DPG methods due to distinct mechanisms and influences such as biological activity, landforms, or extraction procedures, etc. In conclusion, while DPG methods are effective for identifying concealed deposits despite their inherent limitations, an integrated DPG strategy is proposed to enhance prospecting reliability and reduce costs in loess-covered regions.

title: Geochemical evolution and therapeutic properties of the Kangbu geothermal springs, Southern Tibet, China
description: Publication date: July 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 204 Author(s): Xiaofei Sun, Hongbing Tan, Zhiwei Shi, Junying Yang, Hongkai Zhu
abstract: Kangbu Geothermal Springs in southern Tibet are well known for their therapeutic properties and long-standing cultural significance. To scientifically elucidate the hydrochemical evolution mechanisms of therapeutic geothermal waters and support integrated development of balneotourism with medical care, this study systematically collected typical geothermal water and river samples for hydrochemical and environmental isotope analysis. Results show that the waters meet therapeutic standards for metasilicic acid-, boron-, and fluoride-rich mineral waters and contain elevated Li, As, Rb, Br, and Mo compared with river water. The potential therapeutic properties of thermal springs are generally attributed to the combined effects of temperature and dissolved chemical constituents. In conjunction with findings from previous biomedical and experimental studies, these constituents of the Kangbu geothermal springs may be associated with cardiovascular health, promotion of skeletal and dental integrity (through enhanced bone growth, density, and fracture healing), support of gastrointestinal and dermatological functions, neurotrophic activity, potential reduction of cancer risk, and roles as essential enzymatic cofactors. The geothermal waters are HCO3·Cl–Na type formed by mixing deep high-temperature fluids with cold water during ascent, with chemistry primarily controlled by silicate dissolution. Stable isotopes indicate recharge mainly from high-altitude precipitation and snowmelt between 6473.88 and 6687.75 m. Silica–enthalpy modeling yields estimated reservoir temperatures ranging from 236.88 to 269.74 °C, cold-water fractions ranging from 82.02% to 86.99%, and circulation depths ranging from 3.92 to 4.65 km. These results indicate a high-temperature geothermal system sustained by deep circulation and water–rock interaction, highlighting its potential for long-term utilization.

title: Hydrothermal processes and their effects in the precipitation, textures and isotopic composition of calcite and anhydrite, Irruputuncu Volcano case study
description: Publication date: July 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 204 Author(s): Christian Betancourt, Diego Morata
abstract: Understanding fluid sources and processes in hydrothermal systems is an important topic of their characterization, allowing us to recognize fluid pathways and mineralization patterns. In this sense, we studied the Irruputuncu hydrothermal system, a relatively unique system not only due to the characteristics of its location, the Chilean Altiplano, but also because of its proximity to the Coposa Salt Flat. Through the analysis of alteration minerals and their isotopic compositions sampled from two geothermal exploration wells, we measured δ18O and δ13C in calcites and δ18O and δ34S in anhydrites. Both minerals occur predominantly as open spaces fillings along the two geothermal exploration boreholes, PGC-01 (800 m long) and PGC-02 (1430 m long). We complemented these isotopic data with a thorough characterization of calcite and anhydrite textures along both wells using petrography and scanning electron microscopy (SEM), including cathodoluminescence (SEM-CL) and punctual chemical analyses by energy-dispersive X-ray spectrometry (SEM-EDX). Measured anhydrite samples showed isotopic compositions ranging from −3‰VSMOW to 14.2‰VSMOW δ18O and −9‰CDT to 19.8‰CDT δ34S, while calcites ranged from 6.8‰VSMOW to 13.98‰VSMOW δ18O and −4.81‰VPDB to 0.1‰VPDB δ13C. Mineral textures were varied, with calcites showing predominantly rhombic, massive, jigsaw or crustiform textures, and sometimes a combination of them. Anhydrites were predominantly massive, blocky or bladed, and we recognized distinct growth patterns when observed with SEM-CL. Crystals from the shallower levels of the system show growth patterns consisting of a combination of lamellar cores and concentrical rims, while deeper samples present anhydrites with exclusively lamellar patterns. From these results, we propose that mineralization in the deepest zones of the geothermal system is controlled exclusively by the boiling of an already mixed hydrothermal fluid, which during its ascent, is submitted to a combination of boiling and mixing processes, with both processes controlling the mineral precipitation at different stages. This is also supported by isotopic modelling of δ18O, which not only shows that the isotopic distribution requires a combination of both boiling and mixing between magmatic and meteoric fluids, but also that the hydrothermal fluids are comprised of approximately 36% meteoric fluids in the deeper zones of the system, and up to 96% in the shallower areas. We also propose that lamellar growth patterns in anhydrites can help recognize boiling stages within their formation, as well as changes in mineralization conditions.

title: Quantifying the effects of geogenic contaminated groundwater on water quality of Ulansuhai lake, Hetao Basin, China
description: Publication date: July 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 204 Author(s): Ruyi Liu, Kun Qian, Hua He, Caixia Li, Honglie Jiang, Junxia Li, Xianjun Xie
abstract: Accurately identifying groundwater-surface water interactions along lake shorelines in arid and semi-arid regions is essential for assessing lake water quality and ecosystem health. In this study, a total of 133 water samples—including groundwater, surface water, lake water, and pore water—were collected from the irrigation area of the Hetao Basin and Ulansuhai lake to analyze typical ion concentrations, as well as stable isotopic compositions. Combined with a 222Rn mass balance model, the rates of groundwater-surface water interaction and the input fluxes of inferior-quality components along approximately 10 km of the western shoreline of Ulansuhai lake were quantified. The results indicate that Na–Cl type was the dominant hydrogeochemical type of groundwater, and the groundwater discharge rates ranged from 9.03 to 174.3 mm/d, with a mean value of 48.11 mm/d. Lacustrine groundwater discharge (LGD) displayed significant spatial heterogeneity, with the maximum rate being 19.3 times greater than the minimum. Moreover, higher discharge rates were predominantly observed along convex shoreline segments, where the average LGD rate was 2.48 times that along concave shorelines. Based on field investigations and previous studies, we infer that the spatial pattern of groundwater discharge in this area is primarily controlled heterogeneity of regional groundwater flow. The sensitivity analysis revealed that lake water 222Rn, groundwater 222Rn, and wind speed, were key drivers influencing the estimated LGD rates from the 222Rn mass balance model. This study provides new insights into the processes governing the input of inferior-quality groundwater components into large lakes in arid and semi-arid regions.

title: The occurrence of parent and substituted polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons in the interconnected river-lake system of Wuhan
description: Publication date: July 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 204 Author(s): Biru Hou, Tingting Li, Zefan Wang, Ruiqi Wang, Jiawei Zhang, Lihao Zhi, Chang Pu, Shihua Qi, Lingzhi Tan, Chengkai Qu
abstract: Parent polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PPAHs) and substituted polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (SPAHs), recognized as pervasive carcinogenic pollutants, pose significant threats to both ecosystems and human health. This study presents a systematic investigation into the pollution characteristics, source apportionment, and risk assessment of PPAHs and SPAHs (3 Methyl-PAHs and 4 Oxygenated-PAHs) within the surface waters of the Wuhan watershed. The results showed that the concentration of the sum of the concentrations of 16 PPAHs (∑16PPAHs) and the 7 SPAHs (∑7SPAHs) were from 0.7 to 2553.3 ng/L and from 0 to 1681.6 ng/L, respectively, with a pronounced dominance of the 3 and 4 ring components. Source analysis identified coal/biomass combustion as the principal source of contamination, alongside notable contributions from shipping leakage, industrial emissions, and the secondary formation pathway of SPAHs. Ecological risk assessment indicated that while the overall risk was generally manageable, specific localized points (e.g., MLN05, NL09) presented elevated ecological risks. The health risk assessment indicated that the equivalent toxic equivalent of benzo[a]pyrene (TEQPAHs) reached a maximum of 14.8 ng/L, and the carcinogenic risk through skin exposure for children was worthy of attention. The study also found that the spatial distribution of individual risk (ILCR) and population risk (PCI) was not completely consistent. The PCI was higher in the inner ring area due to the dense population. Overall, the regional impact of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons in the Wuhan River Basin was relatively low, and this study provided scientific basis for implementing precise pollution control.

title: Sources and biodegradation potential of naphthenic acids in an oil sands pit-lake
description: Publication date: July 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 204 Author(s): Mohamed El-Waraky, David Bowman, Robert K. Nelson, Christopher M. Reddy, Lesley Warren, Gregory F. Slater
abstract: Naphthenic acids (NAs) are some of the most hazardous components of oil sands tailings and thus understanding their fate is an important component of the reclamation of oil sand sites. Syncrude Canada Ltd. has undertaken the first full-scale pilot reclamation of oil sands tailings using water-capped tailing technology via the commissioning of a pit lake, Base Mine Lake (BML). Understanding the presence and persistence of NAs in the water column of BML is integral to assessment of the overall functioning of the lake and its water quality. This study applied comprehensive two-dimensional gas chromatography mass spectrometry to investigate the sources and biodegradation potential of select chromatographically well-resolved NAs in the BML water column over a period of four years. Temporal analysis of analyzed NAs in the water column revealed a consistent profile of NAs species and isomer distributions across the four years of the study. Comparison of relative abundances of NAs in potential sources (bitumen, oil sands process water (OSPW), and fluid fine tailings (FFT)) versus the water column yielded a molecular fingerprint consistent with a mixed input of NAs into the BML water column from both FFT and water column associated processes. Elevated FFT NAs abundances relative to the water column implies that FFT represents an ongoing source to the water column via advection, diffusion or ebullition-related transport. The observation of 14 unique NAs isomers exclusively present in the water column, however, implied another source which we propose is the ongoing biodegradation of hydrocarbons within the BML water column. The temporal consistency of the BML NAs relative abundance profiles, implies that their biodegradation within the water column mitigates the continual input of NAs, whether transported via advection from FFT or generated through water column hydrocarbon precursor biodegradation. Consequently, the water column serves as dynamic buffer potentially limiting the redistribution of NAs within BML.

title: Geochemical, mineralogical and particle-size controls on origin, transport and storage of sediment-associated metal(loid)s in an acid mine drainage-affected river
description: Publication date: July 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 204 Author(s): Elin Jennings, Patrizia Onnis, Rich Crane, William M. Mayes, Adam P. Jarvis, Karen A. Hudson-Edwards
abstract: Acid mine drainage (AMD) continues to contaminate river systems worldwide, yet the interactions of metal(loid)s with sediments and the controls on their storage and remobilisation remain poorly constrained. This study examines the geochemical and mineralogical factors governing sediment-associated As, Cu, and Zn along an AMD-impacted river system (Carnon River, UK). To assess the interaction of metal(loid)s in sediments, their mineral hosts, and distribution over different particle sizes were investigated. Sediment concentrations reached 8210 mg/kg As, 5040 mg/kg Cu, 2760 mg/kg Zn, and 137,000 mg/kg Fe, substantially above guideline values and persisting downstream of the initial AMD input. Sulfide and sulfate minerals hosted Zn and Fe oxides were the primary hosts for As and Cu. Arsenic was strongly correlated with Fe, suggesting association with secondary Fe-oxide. Elevated downstream concentrations of such ecotoxic metal(loid)s within sediments indicated continuous input from both AMD precipitation and remobilised historic waste and limited natural attenuation. This integrated approach reveals a bimodal distribution: sorption/co-precipitation with secondary Fe-oxide or coarse sulfide sources that sustained contamination decades after mining ceased. These findings demonstrate how sediment mineralogy and particle size dictate contaminant mobility and long-term storage in AMD-affected catchments.

title: Coupled hydrogeochemical, isotopic, and microclimatic processes driving modern carbonate precipitation in a southwestern Iberian karst system
description: Publication date: July 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 204 Author(s): Bryan Salgado-Almeida, Concepción Jiménez de Cisneros, Aránzazu Peña, Manuel López-Chicano, Antonio González-Ramón, Wenceslao Martín-Rosales
abstract: Understanding carbonate precipitation in caves requires integrating hydrological, geochemical and microclimatic processes operating across the soil–epikarst–cave continuum. Here we present a multi-year (2018–2025) monitoring dataset from Gruta de las Maravillas (SW Spain), combining environmental measurements, hydrochemistry, stable isotopes (δ18O, δ2H, δ13C), surface soils, and modern carbonate precipitates. Results show that carbonate precipitation is primarily controlled by the coupling between cave ventilation and hydrological processes. Seasonal ventilation driven by external–internal temperature gradients regulates cave-air CO2 concentrations, which in turn control carbonate supersaturation of cave waters, particularly dripwaters. Hydrochemical data indicate dominant carbonate dissolution during infiltration, with spatial variability linked to flow paths and residence time, and evidence for episodic prior calcite precipitation along specific pathways. Dripwater isotopic compositions reflect meteoric recharge dominated by winter precipitation, with short-term variability generally attenuated during transfer through the soil and epikarst, although occasional recharge events may transmit less damped signals. Measured and calculated δ18O values of modern calcite are in close agreement, consistent with near-equilibrium fractionation under the monitored cave conditions, although transient kinetic effects associated with short-term changes in drip rate and/or degassing conditions cannot be excluded. These results provide a process-based characterization of how ventilation, recharge and subsurface transfer jointly control carbonate precipitation and isotopic signals in this monitored karst system, providing constraints for the interpretation of modern cave carbonates and speleothem-based paleoclimate reconstructions.

title: Brillouin spectroscopy as a proxy for fluid inclusion salinity in gypsum: application to brine evolution in a sebkha system
description: Publication date: July 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 204 Author(s): Wiem Ben Aissa, Niels Brall, Véronique Gardien, Mouna El Mekki-Azouzi, Rania Ben Aissa, Mohamed Ali Tagorti, Frédéric Caupin
abstract: Evaporitic deposits constitute valuable archives of paleoenvironmental conditions in arid regions, where other sedimentary records are scarce. Reconstructing the salinity of parent brines from evaporite minerals, such as gypsum, is therefore essential for understanding past hydrological and climatic regimes. This study evaluates Brillouin spectroscopy as a non-destructive proxy for quantifying the salinity of fluid inclusions. Sound velocity measurements were performed on monophasic and biphasic fluid inclusions hosted in Middle Holocene gypsum from the el Melah sebkha (southeastern Tunisia) and were compared with bulk salinity estimates obtained by microthermometry. Calibration of sound velocity was achieved using a natural brine of known salinity, from which a range of solutions was produced through controlled evaporation and dilution experiments. The results reveal a robust linear relationship between sound velocity and salinity for both experimental brines (up to 320 g/L) and gypsum-hosted fluid inclusions. Bulk salinities reconstructed by microthermometry range from 23.1 to 28.5 wt %, consistent with gypsum precipitation from modern marine-derived brines. Salinities derived from Brillouin sound velocity measurements closely match microthermometric estimates, with deviations of 0.5-1.3% using fluid inclusion calibration equations and 0.4-4.8% using synthetic brine calibrations. These results demonstrate that Brillouin spectroscopy provides a reliable and accurate proxy for salinity determination in gypsum fluid inclusions and offers significant advantages in systems where conventional microthermometry is time consuming and/or limited by metastability effects or complex brine compositions.

title: Impact of soil microbial processes on the fate of crude oil contamination: Insights from aerobic and anaerobic microcosms
description: Publication date: July 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 204 Author(s): Rakiya Muhammad, Christopher Boothman, Hokyung Song, Jonathan R. Lloyd, Bart E. van Dongen
abstract: Niger Delta oil spills significantly impact the local ecosystem, potentially affecting soil microbial communities that are vital for various functional processes, including bioremediation. Here soils from a recent oil spill were used to conduct microcosm experiments under aerobic and anaerobic conditions amended with different terminal electron acceptors (TEAs) to assess the oil contamination bioremediation potential using in situ microbial communities. Results showed a substantial increase in hydrocarbon removal, with the highest removal efficiency observed in aerobic microcosms and anaerobic microcosms when sulfate or iron (III) were used as TEA. In contrast to aerobic conditions anaerobic conditions resulted in the release of Fe and Al into solution.
