abstract: Global climate change is expected to intensify extreme weather events, leading to an increase in the frequency and severity of rainfall-induced landslides. However, future trends in landslide susceptibility remain unclear. In this study, we constructed three models: Random Forest (RF), eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) by integrating the global historical landslide catalog with both dynamic and static environmental factors. The models achieved AUC values of 0.91, 0.88, and 0.92, respectively, with the CNNs model performing best. Thus, CNNs was used for future landslide susceptibility prediction. Using 2021 as the baseline, the global landslide susceptibility distribution for 2050 and 2100 was predicted using three Shared Socioeconomic Pathway (SSP) scenarios from the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6). The results show that the areas that are susceptible to landslides in 2050 and 2100 are primarily located in tropical and subtropical mountainous regions, characterized by high rainfall and steep terrain. In contrast, areas with lower landslide susceptibility are concentrated in plains, deserts, and temperate regions. Higher emission scenarios continue to amplify landslide risks, significantly increasing very high susceptibility by 177%-209% from 2050 to 2100, while low susceptible areas remain dominant (>75%) across all scenarios. Six continents exhibit different characteristics of change. These findings quantify future trends in global landslide susceptibility under different scenarios, providing a scientific basis and decision support for countries to develop scenario-based disaster early warning systems and adaptive policies.

title: Microbial carbon pump promotes refractory organic carbon accumulation in karst waters: Coupled responses of bacterial communities and dissolved organic matter under thermal stratification
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 676 Author(s): Jia Qin, Xinlu Su, Yikun Jia, Peng Chen, Qiufang He, Wen Lai, Tao Zhang, Jianhong Li, Junbing Pu
abstract: Inland waters are vital to the global carbon cycle, yet bacterial-driven carbon sequestration in karst aquatic systems with intense carbonate weathering and high dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC) concentrations remains unclear. This study examines a typical karst reservoir in southwestern China, combining seasonal field sampling and in situ microbial incubation experiments to investigate the bacterial-driven transformation of dissolved organic carbon (DOC) into refractory dissolved organic carbon (RDOC) in karst waters. The results show that thermal stratification creates vertically heterogeneous microenvironments, significantly influencing dissolved organic matter (DOM) composition and bacterial community structure. Bacteria–DOM coupling varies across layers, with the thermocline serving as a key zone for DOM transformation. During the strong thermal stratification (STS) period, RDOC conversion efficiency is approximately 2.6 times higher than during the isothermal mixing (IM) and early thermal stratification (ETS) periods. Overall, thermal stratification regulates microhabitats and bacterial community structure, while high DIC concentrations enhance carbon substrate supply; together, these factors promote the activity of the microbial carbon pump (MCP) in karst waters. This study reveals the potential for RDOC accumulation in karst aquatic systems and confirms their role as an important microbially driven “hidden carbon sink”.

title: Neural operator-based multi-objective optimization for spatiotemporal data-informed seepage parameter identification: a case study on deep overburden in a dam foundation
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 676 Author(s): Libo Wang, Weijun Cen, Bo Liu, Jiahao Qian, Changhai Zheng
abstract: Accurate identification of seepage parameters for deep overburden in dam foundations is critical for reliable seepage analysis and safety evaluation. Conventional identification approaches remain constrained by single-time-point conditions, incomplete spatial coverage of engineering information, and two-dimensional domains, which may result in biased parameter estimates. This study proposes a spatiotemporal data-informed seepage parameter identification framework that integrates a deep operator network (DeepONet) surrogate with an improved multi-objective coati optimization algorithm (IMOCOA). Time-varying water levels and spatially distributed (left bank, riverbed, and right bank) monitoring data from multiple seepage-pressure points are fused into a unified multi-objective formulation. DeepONet is conditioned on physics-informed spatial descriptors, enabling operator learning of the mapping from seepage parameters to spatiotemporal pressure responses, and achieving high prediction fidelity (R 2 = 0.994–0.999). The optimization efficiency of IMOCOA is enhanced by the Sobol initialization, dynamic β-η learning, and ε-dominance-based truncation, achieving a low inverted generational distance (0.109) and a high hypervolume (0.539). A reliability-informed weighting strategy considering engineering preference is proposed to extract a representative compromise solution from Pareto alternatives. The framework is validated on a rockfill dam founded on deep overburden with a thickness of 148 m, and the identified parameters reproduce observed seepage-pressure evolution and yield physically consistent seepage behavior. Comparative analyses demonstrate that the framework achieves higher computational efficiency and robustness for seepage parameter identification by explicitly integrating domain-specific physical information, demonstrating its potential for broader application in complex geotechnical and hydraulic engineering problems.

title: Towards more accurate streamflow and flood prediction via explainable CNN-LSTM: leveraging ERA5 gridded precipitation and hydrological observations through input-architecture co-design
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 676 Author(s): Sheng Huang, Tianyi Nan, Yueling Wang
abstract: Deep learning has achieved high accuracy in hydrological and hydrodynamic modeling, yet effectively incorporating ungauged, precipitation-driven lateral small tributaries into model architectures for more accurate streamflow prediction remains underexplored. This challenge is particularly pronounced under spatially heterogeneous rainfall, where dimensional mismatches between gridded precipitation data and sparse upstream observations hinder accurate source-sink representation. Here, we propose an integrated framework that combines a three-dimensional Convolutional Neural Network (3D-CNN) with a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network, enabling flexible fusion of gridded precipitation (e.g., ERA5) and upstream hydrological observations. The proposed 3D-CNN-LSTM model incorporating richer spatiotemporal precipitation information yields more accurate and stable streamflow and flood predictions across most stations compared to models using only upstream streamflow and spatially averaged precipitation. Even where precipitation-driven tributary inflows account for as little as 5% of downstream flow, the model improves flood prediction in 80% of events relative to a streamflow-only LSTM. When such tributary inflows contribute positively to downstream streamflow, incorporating spatially distributed precipitation through the 3D-CNN-LSTM leads to improved predictions, even under complex river–lake interactions. In contrast, when precipitation acts as irrelevant or uninformative inputs (e.g., under flow diversion with complex routing pathways), the streamflow-only LSTM architecture performs adequately without the added precipitation noise. Explainable deep learning techniques further provide diagnostic insights into the 3D-CNN-LSTM model’s sensitivity to lagged upstream inputs and reveal patterns that are broadly consistent with known hydrological behavior. This integrated input-architecture co-design strengthens deep learning’s capacity to uncover and interpret streamflow generation mechanisms.

title: Modifying the WRF-Noah irrigation representation to simulate regional climate effects of irrigation over the humid middle-lower Yangtze Plain, China
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 676 Author(s): Liangfeng Zou, Dongguo Shao, Yuanyuan Zha, Yuqing Diao, Jiong Zhu, Shu Chen, Wenquan Gu, Mengzi Li
abstract: Exploring the climatic effects of agricultural irrigation and potential mechanisms is essential for guiding sustainable irrigation development. However, the impacts of irrigation on the climate of the humid Middle-Lower Yangtze Plain (MLYP) region in China, a global hotspots of irrigation, remain unclear. The region employs intricate rotation patterns, with paddy as the primary crop cultivated in inundated fields. Due to the simplification of differentiated irrigation for various crops and paddy ponding irrigation in land surface models, realistically modeling irrigation practices in the MLYP is challenging. Therefore, this study developed a subgrid-scale multi-crop demand-driven irrigation scheme and coupled it with the Weather Research and Forecasting-Noah (WRF-Noah) model, incorporating a new ponding submodule to simulate water and energy budget processes in paddy field subgrids. Two experiments (irrigation on and off) were designed to explore the impacts and mechanisms of irrigation on the regional climate of MLYP. Results indicate that the modified scheme improved the simulation accuracy of surface fluxes, soil moisture, and irrigation amount. Irrigation significantly increased latent heat flux, leading to domain-averaged cooling of 0.316°C during spring and summer, while the irrigated subgrids reached 0.647°C. Reduced planetary boundary layer height strengthened atmospheric stability and suppressed summer local convective precipitation over MLYP. Irrigation-induced anomalous anticyclone and large-scale circulation perturbation inhibited internal moisture convergence and external imports, reducing summer non-convective precipitation. Our study emphasizes the critical importance of realistic irrigation representation in climate studies and advances the mechanism-level understanding that water management modulates land–atmosphere interactions.

title: Sediment hysteresis loop variability in watersheds during rainfall-runoff erosion: effects of internal watershed controls revealed by process-based modeling
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 676 Author(s): Seonghyeon Hong, Soyoung Kim, Dae-Hong Kim
abstract: Sediment hysteresis loops are widely employed to interpret watershed erosion responses; however, their high variability between events has raised concerns about their reliability as consistent indicators. This study investigates the physical mechanisms controlling hysteresis loop variability using process-based numerical simulations conducted under idealized conditions. Key watershed and hydrological factors, including particle size distribution (PSD), microtopographic features, raindrop impact, and rainfall duration, were systematically varied to isolate their individual and combined effects on sediment dynamics. The simulations demonstrated that, even when discharge hysteresis at the watershed outlet remained consistent, sediment responses diverged substantially depending on internal watershed characteristics. Loop steepness was primarily governed by surface particle size and PSD: fine particles, with higher erodibility and lower settling velocities, generated steeper loops, whereas surface coarsening, driven by selective transport, reduced fine particle availability and flattened the loops. Rotational direction was determined by detachment mechanisms and sediment availability: intense raindrop impact triggered rapid initial mobilization, producing clockwise loops, whereas the absence of raindrop impact promoted overland flow-driven detachment, resulting in positive transport lags and counterclockwise loops. Loop width displayed a clear power-law relationship with the product of the loop gradient and the degree of surface coarsening indices, indicating that these metrics jointly capture the integrated effects of rainfall, soil properties, and microtopography and can infer in-watershed coarsening from outlet signals. Overall, this study provides a process-based, quantitatively supported interpretation of how key hydrological and geomorphological drivers shape the slope, rotation, and width of sediment hysteresis loops under shallow overland-flow conditions.

title: Enhancing understanding of vegetation responses to flash droughts: the need for high-temporal-resolution monitoring data
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 676 Author(s): Zixuan Qi, Yuchen Ye, Yanpeng Cai, Chaoxia Yuan, Qian Tan, Lian Sun, Zhifeng Yang, Guanhui Cheng
abstract: Flash droughts, characterized by rapid declines in soil moisture, have become increasingly frequent and exert sustained pressure on terrestrial carbon and water cycles. However, a practical framework is still lacking to systematically track vegetation ecosystems’ coupled structural and functional responses before, during, and after flash-drought onset. We integrate daily observations of the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI), gross primary productivity (GPP), water-use efficiency (WUE), and underlying WUE (uWUE) for China from 1982 to 2019, and use these data to develop a high-temporal-resolution Vegetation Flash Drought Response Framework (HTR-VFDRF). The framework characterises three sequential lag windows: the negative anomaly response time, peak point time, and lag recovery time. Furthermore, we applied the KDE method to analyze the temporal patterns of vegetation structural and functional response sensitivity under flash drought stress, while also employing interpretable machine learning and the geographic detector to analyze the multidimensional drivers of land surface, meteorological, and land–atmosphere coupling factors that influence the negative anomaly peak points in vegetation structure and function. Our results show that vegetation ecosystem functional indicators are more sensitive to flash drought than structural indicators. Preceding and following flash drought events, the vegetation ecosystem function daily-scale negative anomaly response curves exhibit a rapid V-shaped decline and subsequent recovery in humid southeastern China, in contrast to a more gradual S-shaped increase and stabilization in cold-dry and semi-arid regions. Negative anomaly peaks in GPP, WUE, and uWUE deepen from arid to humid zones along a climatic aridity gradient, with mixed forests exhibiting the highest functional stability among vegetation types. Mechanistic analysis reveals that across both monsoon and non-monsoon regions of China, flash drought-induced declines in vegetation carbon uptake are primarily driven by synergistic shifts in soil moisture, air temperature, and surface energy fluxes (SSHF and SLHF), which jointly constrain evapotranspiration and photosynthetic efficiency. Moreover, the interaction between flash-drought intensity and bedrock depth explains approximately 70% of the spatial heterogeneity in long-term mean GPP negative anomaly peak points. These findings emphasize the essential role of high-temporal-resolution monitoring for detecting early functional decline and recovery, and demonstrate that the HTR-VFDRF can serve as a scalable method for evaluating global vegetation resilience and vulnerability to flash drought under continued climate warming.

title: Capturing temporal shifts in forest soil-atmosphere feedbacks: evidence from a Mediterranean catchment
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 676 Author(s): Ilenia Murgia, Christian Massari, Matteo Verdone, Konstantinos Kaffas, David Labat, Daniele Penna
abstract: This study explores the complex interactions among eco-hydro-meteorological ( E H M ) variables, such as soil moisture ( S M ), precipitation ( P ), vapor pressure deficit ( V P D ), and sap flow velocity ( S F ), in the Mediterranean climate, where water scarcity and the effects of climate change are becoming increasingly pronounced. While previous studies have identified thresholds controlling runoff generation in Mediterranean catchments, it remains unclear how lead-lag dynamics among EHM variables govern ecological responses. This study addresses this gap by using wavelet analysis to explore the controls and dynamics of F S M − P and F S M − V P D feedbacks across different time and frequency scales, investigating whether EHM interactions exhibit evident thresholds that trigger feedback switches in response to SM availability and atmospheric demand. These dynamics were studied during the 2021 growing season at two topographic positions (riparian and hillslope) on an experimental hillslope in a Mediterranean forested catchment, central Italy. Our results revealed that SM in the hillslope position showed rapid, event-driven responses to P, with soil water recharge processes that differed significantly between the wet and dry seasons. This sensitivity to climatic forcings was greater in the hillslope SM than in the riparian one, which was characterized by more uniform and smoothed responses. Furthermore, the results highlighted the activation of proactive water-saving strategies adopted by trees located in the hillslope position, as evidenced by a critical SM threshold of 0.15 m 3 / m 3 below which not only was P ineffective, but also SF was severely limited. In contrast, the constant availability of soil water in riparian areas allowed trees to maintain higher transpiration rates, showing a more passive response to atmospheric demand. In conclusion, although P is the main source of soil water recharge, its effectiveness on water availability and tree transpiration depends on complex interactions within the soil-plant-atmosphere continuum, with topography acting as the dominant controlling factor. These insights are critical for improving our understanding of the resilience of forest ecosystems and for guiding more effective water and forest management strategies.

title: Scale-aware triple collocation: optimizing spatiotemporal windows for enhanced multi-source fusion of meteorological data
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 676 Author(s): Zhixin Peng, Lingjie Li, Yintang Wang, Guoqing Wang, Yong Liu, Zhaode Yun, Rui Gao, Leizhi Wang, Xin Su
abstract: Triple Collocation (TC) is a widely adopted approach for multi-source data fusion in meteorological variable estimation, particularly in areas lacking ground-based observations. However, a significant limitation of TC is its inability to account for nonstationary spatiotemporal errors, which can considerably degrade estimation accuracy. Although the previously introduced Dual Time-Space Triple Collocation (TC-2D) accounts for errors nonstationary in either time or space alone, it still overlooks the influence of the spatiotemporal domain scale on fusion performance. To address this limitation, this study proposes two novel fusion frameworks applied to estimate potential evapotranspiration in the middle and upper reaches of the Yellow River Basin: (1) a dynamic TC-2D utilizing localized spatial and temporal slice data (TC-2D-LST), and (2) a three-dimensional TC that incorporates neighborhood-based spatiotemporal information (TC-3D). Results indicate that the fusion accuracy is more sensitive to the temporal window of nonstationary errors than to their spatial window in both methods. By employing optimal window settings, both proposed frameworks achieve improved Kling-Gupta Efficiency (KGE’) values at over two-thirds of the stations compared to TC-2D. Specifically, the daily KGE’ shows an increase from 0.695 to 0.725 or higher, while the pentad-scale value surpasses 0.774, rising from 0.717. Furthermore, TC-3D demonstrated comparable or superior accuracy to TC-2D-LST, even with smaller windows, thus offering a more computationally efficient solution. Overall, the proposed dynamic and localized fusion frameworks extend the applicability of TC, provide a robust, generalizable, and transferable method for multi-source meteorological data integration.

title: Integrating hydraulic processes and graph neural networks for event-scale river morphodynamics
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 676 Author(s): Pin-Chun Huang
abstract: Riverbank erosion is a fundamental process shaping channel morphology, sediment dynamics, and floodplain evolution, yet its prediction remains challenging due to the nonlinear interplay between hydraulic forcing, sediment transport, and geotechnical resistance. Traditional physics-based models grounded in the shallow water equations and the Exner sediment continuity equation provide mechanistic insights but are computationally intensive and sensitive to parameter uncertainties. Conversely, machine learning methods offer rapid and accurate predictions but often lack physical interpretability and generalization. This study introduces a novel spatio-temporal graph neural network (ST-GNN) with a GRU backbone, designed to capture directed hydraulic connectivity and dynamic morphodynamic interactions across a river network. The framework of this research is developed as a surrogate model trained on high-fidelity labels derived from a validated hydromorphodynamic model that explicitly incorporates toe scour, excess-slope failure, and toe-transport mechanisms. This approach enables the ST-GNN to emulate complex morphodynamic responses with high computational efficiency and accuracy, providing a reliable approximation of process-based simulations. The key innovation of this work lies in leveraging a physics-guided graph topology to represent hydraulic connectivity within a machine learning framework. Results demonstrate that the model effectively captures reach-consistent spatio-temporal patterns of bed and bank adjustments. This approach contributes to the predictive science of river morphodynamics by establishing a high-fidelity surrogate that maintains physical consistency while overcoming the computational bottlenecks of traditional numerical solvers.

title: Land use and rainfall drive riverine DOM source dynamics: Insights from spectroscopic and stable carbon isotope analyses
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 676 Author(s): Lunjing Xiao, Zhenzhen Jia, Kaiheng Guo, Yingjie Cao, Jiatang Hu
abstract: Land use and rainfall are key drivers of dissolved organic matter (DOM) dynamics in rivers, yet their coupling effects on DOM sources in heterogeneous urbanized watersheds remain unclear. Here we combine fluorescence spectroscopy and stable carbon isotopes within end-member mixing analysis (EMMA) framework to trace DOM sources along the Guangzhou reach of the Pearl River under contrasting land use and rainfall conditions. The optimized three-dimensional subregional EMMA model (BIX–HIX–δ13C-DOC) substantially outperformed two-dimensional and whole-watershed alternatives, reducing prediction error by 45–50%. Upstream agricultural areas were dominated by soil-derived, humic-rich DOM, whereas midstream and downstream urbanized reaches showed greater wastewater contributions and microbial characteristics. Rainfall increases DOM loads across all zones but variably alters source composition depending on land use. The strongest coupling effect occurs in the midstream agricultural–urban transition zone, where rainfall enhances the surface soil input but decreases the wastewater contribution. By comparison, downstream reaches show minimal source shifts after rainfall, reflecting buffering by continuous wastewater inputs. This study evaluates land use-rainfall interactions on DOM sources, and provides an optimized subregional EMMA approach for DOM source apportionment in tropical and subtropical urban rivers.

title: Partitioning nighttime sap flux into transpiration and stem refilling: Towards improved baselining and sap flux interpretation
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 676 Author(s): Mianzhi Wang, Matti Räsänen, Teemu Hölttä
abstract: Nighttime sap flux is important for understanding tree water-use dynamics in ecohydrological studies, as it represents the diurnal minimum of sap flow and often serves as the reference period for establishing thermal dissipation probe baselines. The baseline indicates simultaneous cessation of both nighttime transpiration and refilling of trees internal water stores. However, finding this moment is challenging as the baseline is dynamically changing, and the complete sap flux cessation may not even occur for boreal forests. Here, we proposed a novel framework using VPD and dendrometer measurements to partition transpiration and refilling from nighttime sap flux density, and introduced a night-by-night baselining scheme that does not rely on identifying the zero-flow moment. One conventional baselining method using the maximum probe voltage (or temperature) difference substantially underestimated sap flux density by 204.56% for nighttime, 28.30% for daytime, and 45.20% for full-day flux in P. sylvestris, and by 344.77%, 45.68%, and 54.76%, respectively, in A. glutinosa. Evaluation through leaf gas exchange and evapotranspiration data confirmed the accuracy of partitioning between nighttime transpiration and refilling, demonstrating that nighttime transpiration can drive measurable nighttime evapotranspiration responses. Seasonally, sap flux density showed an initial increase in both transpiration and refilling, followed by a decline, with transpiration dominating until mid-summer before refilling gradually took precedence.

title: CWN-Net: a precise segmentation model for composite water networks using multi-source and multi-temporal remote sensing imagery
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 676 Author(s): Mingyang Li, Huimin Lei, Fulin Li, Jiwen Huang, Yuzhi Shi, Shangjie Xu, Han Wang, Sinan Wang, Rui Wang, Lili Liu, Suzhen Cheng, Lei Guo, Hongjie Xin, Zhen Yang, Guanghui Wang, Xianhu Guo, Jingjing Sun
abstract: Precise segmentation of composite water networks diverges from conventional water body detection due to challenges like intermittent channel flows, spectral confusion from aquatic or riparian vegetation obscuring waterways or dry riverbeds, morphological heterogeneity, and limitations of existing datasets. To address these, this study proposes CWN-Net, a high-fidelity model leveraging multi-source (Sentinel-1 SAR, Sentinel-2 multispectral) and multi-temporal remote sensing imagery. Built on U-Net, it integrates a shared CNN encoder, Swin Transformer module, temporal attention, dual-branch point-area segmentation heads, and consistency loss, enhanced by SHAP for interpretability. Validated in four Shandong Province cities (37,077 km2) as a “natural rivers–artificial channels–agricultural irrigation canals” study area, the datasets incorporate seasonal features. Comparative evaluation against LightGBM, MobileNetV2, DeepLabv3+, SegFormer-B0, Swin-Unet and two others shows CWN-Net, with 2.96 million parameters, achieves Precision 0.9320, F1 Score 0.9408, and IoU 0.8883, outperforming benchmarks in narrow irrigation channels, vegetation-covered regions, and urban shadows. SHAP analysis highlights third-quarter near-infrared and fourth-quarter green bands as primary contributors, with multi-source fusion mitigating SAR speckle noise in dry periods. The generated datasets augment HydroRIVERS and OSM deficiencies, adding 8.22 km urban hidden networks and 86.877 km unlabeled channels/mountainous rivers, providing high-precision support for regional water management, flood risk assessment, and irrigation optimization.

title: Wetlands as a critical water source for local and downwind ecosystems and societies over China through atmospheric moisture transport
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 676 Author(s): Yanhui Chen, Wenhan Pei, Jiping Liu, Xu Lian, Jiangpeng Cui
abstract: Wetlands, as areas permanently or seasonally water-saturated, provide essential ecosystem services both locally and to surrounding regions. However, their impacts on the societies and ecosystems in remote downwind areas through atmospheric moisture transport are poorly understood. Using atmospheric moisture transport data, satellite observations, and socio-economic statistics, here we find that wetlands exert a widespread impact on local and downwind precipitation via terrestrial moisture recycling, which has the potential to support up to 3.5 × 104 km2 of forest growth, and provide freshwater availability for sustaining a gross domestic product (GDP) of 587.8 billion US dollars (USD) and population of 210.3 million over China. More importantly, these benefits of wetlands are mainly realized in downwind regions. For forest growth, GDP, and population, the downwind regions account for 74.1%, 79.1%, and 89.0% of the total effects, respectively. Furthermore, inland wetlands are the major contributors (including local and downwind effects) to forest growth (61.8%) and GDP (67.2%). In contrast, coastal wetlands exhibit the largest contribution to population livelihoods, which accounts for 54.8% of the total contribution. Our findings highlight the critical downwind benefits of wetlands to ecosystems and societies, which have not been widely recognized by the scientific community and public as an increment to known services of wetlands. Our results also imply these benefits may diminish as wetlands degrade under land use and climate change, indicating the urgency for wetland management and conservation in China.

title: Mamba-enhanced multi-scale state space model for robust runoff prediction under data-scarce conditions across climatic zones
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 676 Author(s): Wen-chuan Wang, Tao Zhang, Dong-mei Xu
abstract: To address the problems of constrained data quality, mixed multi-scale characteristics, and low efficiency in long-range dependency modeling in hydrological runoff prediction, this study proposes a Multi-scale Mamba (MSM) model. This model adopts a progressive architecture comprising “multiscale feature extraction – long-range dependency modeling – key information enhancement,” with three core customized modules: a multiscale convolutional-attention fusion block, which simultaneously extracts multiscale runoff features through parallel convolutional branches at different temporal scales and suppresses observational data noise via a cross-scale attention-weighted fusion mechanism; a Residual-Enhanced Mamba block, which efficiently captures long-range hydrological dependencies with linear time complexity based on a selective state-space model, and optimizes gradient propagation in deep networks via residual connections to address training degradation issues; and a temporal attention module, which adaptively focuses on critical time steps of extreme hydrological events to enhance the fitting capability for hydrological extreme events. Experiments are carried out at four hydrological stations, namely Hongshan River, Yingluoxia, Tangnaihai, and Pawcatuck, covering arid, alpine, and temperate humid regions, with comparisons against five mainstream models including Transformer, TCN, GRU, LSTM, and Mamba. The results show that, under conditions of limited data quality and sparse samples, the MSM model achieved an average NSE of 0.918 across four stations, representing an 8.3% improvement over the arithmetic mean of the five baseline models, a 28.51% reduction in RMSE, and a 10.2% increase in KGE; Compared to the original Mamba model, the efficiency of long-range dependency modeling improved by 30%, and the prediction error for extreme runoff events decreased by 17.6%. Compared to existing mainstream methods, the MSM model overcomes the core bottlenecks of traditional models—namely, poor generalization in data-scarce or high-noise scenarios and the difficulty in balancing long-series modeling accuracy with computational efficiency. It demonstrates excellent prediction accuracy and robustness across different climate zones and land surface conditions, providing efficient and reliable technical support for hydrological runoff prediction in data-scarce basins.

title: Multi-scale spatiotempral characterization and trend analysis of meteorological and geographical characteristics of drought in India’s arid and semi-arid regions
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 676 Author(s): Kandula Bharghavi, Thotli Lokeswara Reddy, Hemalatha Kapa, Penti Rajesh, Renati Siddi Raju, Krishnareddigari Krishna Reddy
abstract: Drought is a complex and pervasive climate hazard that significantly affects agricultural productivity, water resources, and socioeconomic conditions. While numerous studies have analyzed drought in India at national or state scales, there is limited understanding of its evolution across distinct arid and semi-arid sub-climatic zones, particularly the hot and cold arid and semi-arid regions, which are highly vulnerable to climate variability and rising temperatures. To address this gap, the present study conducts a comprehensive, multi-scale spatiotemporal assessment of drought characteristics using the Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI) and the Standardized Precipitation Evapotranspiration Index (SPEI) from 1981 to 2020. Drought duration, frequency, and intensity were quantified at 1-, 3-, 6-, 12-, and 24-month temporal resolutions, and trend analysis was performed using the non-parametric Mann-Kendall test and Sen’s slope estimator. Results reveal that SPEI consistently outperforms SPI in capturing prolonged droughts, especially at longer temporal scales, due to its sensitivity to temperature-driven evapotranspiration. Drought frequency generally increases with temporal scale, with the Hot Semi-Arid zone exhibiting the highest frequency at 24 months, while the Cold Arid region shows comparatively lower frequencies. Spatial trends indicate rising drought duration in northern cold zones and decreasing intensity in parts of the Hot Arid zone. Moderate droughts dominate most regions, whereas severe and extreme events intensify at longer scales, particularly in hot semi-arid areas. Significant interannual variability is observed in both SPI and SPEI anomalies, highlighting the vulnerability of arid regions to prolonged dry periods. The correlation between SPI and SPEI strengthens with increasing temporal scale, reflecting the growing influence of evapotranspiration under warming conditions. This study is among the first in India to systematically compare SPI and SPEI across all major arid and semi-arid sub-zones and quantify long-term drought characteristics. The findings provide critical insights for effective drought monitoring, risk assessment, and climate adaptation strategies in vulnerable ecosystems.

title: Evaluating precipitation forecasts from the TIGGE via fuzzy mathematics from the perspective of hydrological research
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 676 Author(s): Chenkai Cai, Jing Wang, Yingjie Zhao, Helong Wang, Jianqun Wang, Xinyi Shen
abstract: Three rates are traditionally employed when evaluating precipitation forecasts, i.e., hit rate, miss alarm rate and false alarm rate. These indicators are influenced by the selection of artificial classification standards, wherein unreasonable standards can yield performance over- or underestimation. To overcome this deficiency, three new general indicators, namely, three fuzzy rates, were developed through fuzzy mathematics theory. Three practical examples based on an artificially designed dataset, control forecasts of six global weather centers, global satellite precipitation products and ground-based station data from Zhejiang Province, China, were designed to examine the effects of the three fuzzy rates. The results revealed that these fuzzy rates not only outperform the three traditional rates by distinguishing between precipitation over- and underestimation but are also unaffected by the classification standard. Evaluations of precipitation forecasts from the six centers on the basis of satellite products and station data from global and regional scales indicated that the precipitation forecasts of no single center are always superior to those of the other centers. Moreover, the three traditional rates caused significant underestimation of the precipitation forecast performance. Furthermore, the precipitation forecast performance tended to decrease as the lead time and magnitude increased. In conclusion, the three fuzzy rates are effective indicators for evaluating precipitation forecasts and provide a reference for hydrological forecasting or reservoir regulation. Notably, the membership function of the three fuzzy rates may significantly affect the evaluation results, which may warrant flexible selection depending on the purpose.

title: Process guided graph-based transformer learning for streamflow predictions in data-sparse river basins
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 676 Author(s): Venkatesh Budamala, Sai Vikas Kona, Rajarshi Das Bhowmik, Hyunglok Kim
abstract: Streamflow prediction in data-sparse regions has traditionally relied on process-based hydrological models (PBMs) or hybrid approaches that combine physical modeling with data-driven learning. However, these methods typically require extensive calibration using local observations and detailed knowledge of internal model parameters, which limits their transferability and interpretability when applied to ungauged basins. To address these challenges, we introduce a novel Process-Guided Graph–Transformer (PGT) framework that surrogates PBMs and enhances streamflow prediction in ungauged basins (PUB) using uncalibrated PBM parameters without explicit calibration or optimization. The proposed framework integrates uncalibrated PBM outputs, river network topology, Graph Neural Networks, and Transformers for spatio-temporal learning, and is evaluated across three hydrologically contrasting river basins in India, Australia, and the United States. Results show that PGT consistently improves predictive skill, increasing median KGE from −0.5 to 0.4 for baseline models (SWAT and SWAT-SUFI2) to 0.50–0.75, while maintaining PBIAS within ± 10%, compared with baseline overprediction frequently exceeding 50%. PUB generalization experiments further demonstrate robust skill transfer from gauged to ungauged subbasins, with ΔKGE remaining near 0.0 ± 0.2 across hydrological distances of 0–300 km. Additional analyses indicate improved extreme-event detection (Critical Success Index ≈ 0.8–0.9 compared to 0.4–0.6 for baselines), reliable uncertainty characterization (p-factor: 0.5–1.0 compared to 0.25–0.6 for baselines), and an 8–40 × reduction in computational cost relative to traditional calibration-based approach (SWAT-SUFI2). Overall, these results demonstrate that PGT provides a scalable and process-consistent solution for multi-site streamflow prediction in data-sparse and ungauged regions.

title: Understanding of deep groundwater age characteristics in the Yangtze River Delta through the combined use of 14 C and 81 Kr
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 675 Author(s): Shiang Lu, Zhaojun Xie, Xin Dai, Wei Jiang, Yueqing Xie, Andrew J. Love, Xulong Gong, Guo-Min Yang, Yan Zhang, Lei He, Zheng-Tian Lu, Rongbing Fu, Jichun Wu
abstract: Assessing the replenishment potential of deep confined aquifers is essential for groundwater resource evaluation and management, yet remains challenging due to their concealed nature and hydrogeological heterogeneity. In this study, we integrate 14C and 81Kr dating with inverse-Gaussian transit time distribution (IG-TTD) modeling to quantify deep groundwater age characteristics in the Yangtze River Delta. For the first time, fossil groundwater up to 191 ± 12 ka was identified in Aquifer Ⅳ (>300 m, Neogene confined aquifer). Under the IG-TTD framework, the two Aquifer Ⅳ samples yielded one constrained solution (Γ = 44.2, Δ/Γ = 0.50) and one unresolved case, likely reflecting mixing dominated by an extremely old groundwater component, with contribution from a less old component. Together, these results suggest a substantial fossil-water component and highly limited replenishment in Aquifer Ⅳ. In contrast, Aquifer Ⅲ (150–350 m, Early Pleistocene confined aquifer) shows upper mean ages of 25.3–31.3 ka and relatively narrow TTDs (Δ/Γ = 0.24–0.44), indicating limited dispersion and an age structure consistent with previously reported late-Pleistocene recharge in the region. These findings provide the first direct evidence of exceptionally old groundwater in eastern China revealed by 81Kr and demonstrate that 14C-based apparent ages can remain valid where mixing is limited. More broadly, the combined use of IG-TTD and dual isotopes offers a robust framework for diagnosing age structure and assessing replenishment potential in deep aquifers, with important implications for both paleoclimate reconstruction and the sustainable management of fossil groundwater resources.

title: From sources to risks: A multi-method approach to groundwater hydrogeochemical evolution in the Hotan Oasis of arid inland river basin, Northwest China
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 675 Author(s): Yuehui Wang, Ziyue Yin, Xiaomin Sun, Erkang Zheng, Jieyu Pan, Jianfeng Wu, Jichun Wu
abstract: Pronounced hydrological seasonality and highly dynamic groundwater systems create complex and spatially heterogeneous hydrogeochemical conditions in arid inland river basins. This complexity hampers reliable source–process identification and complicates effective groundwater management. To address these challenges, an integrated multi-method approach was applied, combining self-organizing map (SOM), positive matrix factorization (PMF), hydrochemical diagrams, isotope tracing, and health risk assessment. In the Hotan Oasis, this approach systematically characterized groundwater hydrochemistry and quantified its controlling mechanisms. Groundwater samples were classified into three clusters (C1, C2, C3), representing different hydrochemical patterns. PMF identified six driving factors (F1–F6) with contributions of 46.90%, 20.79%, 9.10%, 8.86%, 7.36%, and 6.99%, indicating that the groundwater composition was jointly controlled by natural hydrogeochemical processes and anthropogenic inputs. Seasonal differences were pronounced: wet-season recharge enhanced dilution and mineral leaching, whereas dry-season conditions intensified evaporation-driven solute enrichment. Agricultural pollution persisted as a background anthropogenic signal. Health risk assessment indicated fluoride (F−) as the primary non-carcinogenic hazard, especially for infants and children, while localized nitrate enrichment also required attention. This study establishes an integrated source–process–risk framework for groundwater evolution in data-limited, process-complex arid inland river basins. The findings provide mechanistic insights and support adaptive water management in fragile oases and other groundwater-dependent dryland environments.

title: Deep learning-based adaptive multi-resolution characterization of CO 2 storage sites from monitoring data
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 675 Author(s): Zhen Qin, Yingxiang Liu, Harun Ates, Behnam Jafarpour
abstract: In geological CO2 storage (GCS), characterization of subsurface properties and CO2 plume migration through inversion of monitoring data is challenging because the subsurface is spatially heterogeneous, leading to high-dimensional parameter fields, while monitoring data are sparse and unevenly distributed. This mismatch between parameter dimensionality and data coverage renders the inverse problem ill-posed, motivating low-dimensional parameterizations that balance model expressiveness with available observational constraints. Furthermore, heterogeneous data coverage calls for multi-resolution representations that enable spatially adaptive updates: coarse-scale adjustments in poorly informed regions and finer-scale detail where measurements provide stronger constraints. Such flexibility is largely absent in existing approaches, which typically employ a single, globally uniform resolution. To address these limitations, we propose a deep learning architecture that learns a spatially structured, multi-resolution latent representation of subsurface properties. The proposed model, termed the multi-resolution spatial autoencoder (MSAE), encodes parameter fields into latent features at multiple resolutions and decodes them to reconstruct permeability models at user-defined resolution levels. Explicit control of model complexity is achieved through a spatially adaptive, multi-resolution masking scheme that selectively activates latent components according to local data support. Building on MSAE, we demonstrate how the proposed parameterization can be coupled with established inversion frameworks—including gradient-based deterministic optimization and ensemble-based methods—to perform spatially adaptive, multi-resolution inversion under sparse monitoring conditions. The framework balances model complexity with available data support, achieving improved reconstruction and long-term plume prediction compared with fixed uniform-resolution parameterizations. Across both deterministic and ensemble-based inversion settings, it reduces overfitting, stabilizes posterior updates in poorly informed regions, and demonstrates the consistent advantages of adaptive multi-resolution representations.

title: Prediction of urban stormwater runoff quality in data-deficient areas using a semi-supervised machine learning framework
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 675 Author(s): Haibin Yan, David Z. Zhu, Mark R. Loewen, Wenming Zhang, Bert van Duin, Khizar Mahmood
abstract: Urban stormwater quality modeling is essential for effective water resource management. Machine learning (ML) provides a powerful tool to capture the complex nonlinear interactions among rainfall, land use, and pollutant behavior, but its performance is often constrained by limited labeled data, defined here as rainfall events with observed event mean concentration (EMC) measurements. This study developed a semi-supervised Random Forest (RF) framework to improve stormwater quality prediction in data-deficient urban catchments by combining labeled data with abundant unlabeled data, referring to rainfall events for which input features are available but EMC observations are limited. Three supervised models (RF-M1, RF-M2, and RF-M3) were first constructed using different combinations of input variables and training datasets from multiple urban catchments to determine the optimal configuration. The best-performing supervised model (RF-M3) integrated multi-catchment datasets and catchment-specific variables, showing slightly reduced training accuracy but better validating and testing performance, demonstrating improved generalization and reduced overfitting. This model was then used to generate pseudo-labels for unlabeled data, forming the basis of the semi-supervised model (RF-Semi). Application to four urban catchments in Calgary, Canada, showed that RF-Semi achieved Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE) values of 0.85 and 0.62 for total suspended solids (TSS), 0.38 and –0.03 for total nitrogen (TN), and 0.68 and 0.62 for total phosphorus (TP) in the validation and testing datasets, respectively. By leveraging abundant rainfall data to enrich the training dataset, the semi-supervised framework effectively reduced dependence on labeled samples, and improved predictive performance under the studied conditions. Rainfall characteristics were consistently the most influential predictors. The proposed approach provides a practical solution for stormwater quality prediction in data-deficient areas under conditions similar to those examined areas in this study, with potential applicability to other regions where rainfall and catchment characteristics are comparable.

title: Declining precipitation frequency may increase vegetation recovery time following extreme drought
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 675 Author(s): Shuai Zhao, Yimin Chen, Yuanzhi Yao, Hao Shi, Hui Zhang, Yang Li
abstract: Under global climate change, drought events have become increasingly frequent and intense, posing growing risks to terrestrial ecosystems and carbon-cycle stability. Quantifying vegetation drought recovery time (DRT) and its controlling factors is therefore crucial for assessing ecosystem resilience and improving carbon-cycle assessments. While DRT is strongly influenced by post-drought precipitation, previous studies have mainly focused on total precipitation (Ptotal), whereas the role of precipitation frequency (Pfreq) remains unresolved. Here, we quantify how Pfreq influences DRT of global natural vegetation following extreme drought during 1982–2022. Extreme drought events were identified using the 3-month Standardized Precipitation–Evapotranspiration Index (SPEI-3), and DRT was defined as the time from maximum Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) suppression to recovery of NDVI anomalies to the long-term mean for two consecutive months. We compared DRT sensitivity to Pfreq versus Ptotal using random-forest (RF) models interpreted with SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP). In the global model, DRT was generally more sensitive to Ptotal than to Pfreq (mean(|SHAP_Pfreq|)/mean(|SHAP_Ptotal|) = 0.67 (0.52–0.79)), although Pfreq remained a substantial predictor. In an RF-based scenario analysis, significant Pfreq declines occurred in 34.29% of naturally vegetated grid cells and were associated with DRT increases in 24.59% of grid cells (≈72% of the Pfreq-decline grid cells). Across vegetation types, mean DRT increases under Pfreq decline ranged from 13.57% to 19.52%. These results indicate that, although precipitation amount remains the dominant global precipitation-related control on drought recovery, precipitation frequency is an important complementary constraint that should be explicitly represented in global recovery assessments under shifting rainfall regimes.

title: Deep learning error post-processing improves stochastic watershed modeling
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 675 Author(s): Benjamin Manoli, Sandeep Poudel, David K. Koval, Sarah Y. Murphy, Scott Steinschneider, Jonathan Lamontagne
abstract: Hydrologic extremes, including floods and droughts, pose substantial societal risks that are expected to intensify with climate change. Deterministic watershed models (DWMs) remain a mainstay for modeling these extremes, but lack explicit representation of uncertainty, limiting their utility for risk-informed planning. Stochastic watershed models (SWMs) address this limitation by generating ensembles of streamflow via models of observed DWM residuals. However, most SWMs struggle with the complex dependence between DWM residuals and the underlying hydrologic state, which can complicate stochastic simulations under nonstationary climates. Deep learning (DL) models, whether used as standalone models or post-processors for process-based DWMs, offer a pathway to address this challenge by reducing conditional dependence. In this study, we evaluate SWMs applied to seven models: three process-based models (PRMS, Hymod, and HBV), their hybrid process-DL counterparts, and a pure DL DWM, focusing on daily simulations and extremes under both historical conditions and synthetic climate change scenarios. Results for a case study watershed in Massachusetts show that SWMs applied to hybrid or pure DL DWMs consistently outperform those applied to process-based DWMs. However, an SWM applied to the pure DL model exhibits weaknesses at low flows for this study basin, underscoring the value of hybrid approaches. Extending the analysis across 73 additional basins demonstrates that these improvements are robust and generalizable statewide. This work highlights the potential of a DL-enhanced stochastic watershed modeling framework to advance hydrologic risk prediction under changing climate conditions, offering a scalable methodology for integrating uncertainty into watershed modeling for long-term planning.

title: Emerging global risks of extreme rain-on-snow events under climate warming
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 675 Author(s): Keke Hu, Gulimire Hanati, Ping Jiao, Sulitan Danierhan, Wenjun Liu, Lei Jin, Jiahui Xie
abstract: Global warming is profoundly altering precipitation regimes and snow cover dynamics, thereby reshaping both the frequency and intensity of rain-on-snow (ROS) events worldwide. Yet the future global risks and driving mechanisms of ROS events under climate warming scenarios remain insufficiently understood. Here, using ERA5-Land and a CMIP6 multi-model ensemble, we establish a global ROS event database covering the period 1950–2100 and characterize its spatiotemporal variability, driving mechanisms, and high-risk regions. We find that, relative to the historical period (1950–2023), future ROS events (2024–2100) will exhibit a contraction in spatial extent but an increase in occurrence frequency, with the most pronounced intensification occurring in mid- to high-elevation regions across the mid- to high-latitude Northern Hemisphere. A conditional probability analysis further reveals a synergistic mechanism among temperature, precipitation, and snow depth: when temperatures approach the 0 °C threshold, rainfall intensifies, and persistent snow cover is present, the likelihood of ROS events increases markedly. The projected rise in ROS events across mid- to high-latitude mountainous regions designates the Tibetan Plateau, the margins of Greenland, eastern and western North America, eastern Asia, and eastern Europe as global hotspots of extreme ROS events risk. These events peak in April and exhibit stronger intensities and higher recurrence under warmer climate scenarios. This study provides new insights into the future evolution of global ROS events in the context of ongoing climate warming.

title: Computer vision-based monitoring of stormwater discharge: proof-of-concept for stage measurements
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 675 Author(s): Mohammad Nooshzadi Motlagh, Sierra Young, Kenneth Chapman, Evelynn Wilcox, François Birgand
abstract: Stormwater systems serve as critical urban drainage infrastructure, maintaining municipal functionality and playing key hydrological and environmental roles. Yet, stormwater outlets are not designed for stormflow monitoring, making traditional contact-based sensors unsuitable for gauging highly variable and turbulent flows. To address this, we propose a computer vision approach that quantifies discharge from near-range images and videos of the outlet. Given the challenges of applying traditional computer vision in natural environments with variable lighting and environmental noise, our method employs a combination of machine learning and computer vision (CV-ML) techniques, leveraging the recognizable geometrical shape of culverts in otherwise very noisy images. Specifically, water stage is obtained through subtracting the extracted shape of the round culvert from the height of empty area above water. Subsequently, image-based measurements are transformed into real-world units by applying a homography transformation calibrated using a checkerboard reference object placed parallel to the outlet. Performance evaluation on a culvert of known dimensions demonstrated ± 1 cm accuracy in approximately 80% of measurements. For water stages evaluated under calm, moderately and turbulent flows, the method estimated, respectively, more than 80% of stages within ± 0.5 cm, more than 80% of stage values within ± 0.75 cm, and 63% of values within ± 1 cm (96% within ± 2 cm). These results show great promise in the use of image-based techniques in difficult and turbulent conditions where no traditional techniques are applicable. They are also the prerequisite for estimations of discharge, for which more work is necessary, and on-going.

title: Study on water infiltration characteristics of surface cracks in shallow-buried tunnels in loess tableland areas
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 675 Author(s): Xiaodong Cheng, Qiuyang Hong, Deiyi Wu, Guodong Shi, Yang Zhou
abstract: Differential settlement above shallow-buried loess tunnels frequently induces surface longitudinal cracks. During rainfall events, these fractures serve as preferential flow paths, fundamentally altering the intrinsic infiltration characteristics of the loess matrix. This study elucidates the infiltration mechanisms associated with construction-induced surface cracks in loess tableland regions via an integrated approach comprising in-situ ponding tests, laboratory experiments, and numerical simulations. The findings reveal that the infiltration process is governed by a synergistic interplay between fracture aperture, hydraulic head, rainfall intensity, and matrix permeability. When rainfall intensity exceeds the saturated hydraulic conductivity of the loess, the resulting surface ponding triggers a transition to preferential flow. For narrower fractures infiltration is primarily dominated by piston flow, as the effective flow path is restricted by fine-particle migration and matric swelling. As the aperture increases—typically within the 2–8 mm range—the flow regime transitions toward fingering or mixed piston-fingered flow. In contrast, macro-fractures exceeding 8 mm facilitate rapid, deep-seated preferential infiltration, bypassing the matrix. Furthermore, the upper 1 m of the soil profile exhibits high sensitivity to evaporation, characterized by a “spiral downward” moisture oscillation with alternating phases of depletion and recovery. These insights provide a robust theoretical framework for the risk assessment and mitigation of water-induced hazards in loess tunnel engineering.

title: The hidden buffering: How carbonate geology and sediments suppress CO 2 emissions from reservoirs
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 675 Author(s): Xuan Hu, Wanfa Wang, Xixi Lu, Hongkai Qi, Amit Kumar, Dengming He, Shijun Tu, Yufei Bao, Jie Zeng, Qixin Wu, Hao Xia, Yuchun Wang, Si-Liang Li
abstract: Research on carbon cycling in Qinghai–Tibet Plateau rivers has attracted considerable attention. However, the role of carbonate buffering in regulating carbon dioxide (CO2) dynamics within cascade reservoirs remains poorly understood, particularly in plateau regions characterized by carbonate-rich geology and high suspended sediment concentration (SSC). In carbonate-enriched sediments, carbonate buffering prolongs the equilibration timescales of both partial pressure of CO2 (pCO2) and stable isotopic composition of dissolved inorganic carbon (δ13CDIC) with the atmosphere by ∼10-fold and ∼100-fold, respectively, compared to non-buffered scenarios. Over extended timescales, water-carbonate interactions effectively limit the evasion of metabolically produced CO2 in cascade reservoirs of the Lancang River, reducing CO2 emissions flux (F CO2) by 24.4%. This buffering effect is particularly pronounced in the hypolimnion, where increased carbonate dissolution occurs, and remains sustained in the outflows. Globally, carbonate-dominated reservoirs with high SSC exhibit 82% lower F CO2 than those with low SSC, demonstrating that suspended sediments critically amplify carbonate buffering’s suppression of CO2 emissions. These findings highlight the necessity of incorporating coupled geological and sedimentary processes into global carbon budgets and climate assessments, particularly in high-altitude regions.

title: An end-to-end differentiable, graph neural network-embedded pore network model for permeability prediction
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 675 Author(s): Qingqi Zhao, Heng Xiao
abstract: Accurate prediction of permeability in porous media is essential for modeling subsurface flow. While pure data-driven models offer computational efficiency, they often lack generalization across scales and do not incorporate explicit physical constraints. Pore network models (PNMs), on the other hand, are physics-based and efficient but rely on idealized geometric assumptions to estimate pore-scale hydraulic conductance, limiting their accuracy in complex structures. To overcome these limitations, we present an end-to-end differentiable hybrid framework that embeds a graph neural network (GNN) into a PNM. In this framework, the analytical formulas used for conductance calculations are replaced by GNN-based predictions derived from pore and throat features. The predicted conductances are then passed to the PNM solver for permeability computation. In this way, the model avoids the idealized geometric assumptions of PNM while preserving the physics-based flow calculations. The GNN is first pretrained to regress PNM conductances from local pore and throat features, and is then fine-tuned using a single scalar permeability, avoiding the need for DNS derived pore-scale labels. This is made possible by backpropagating gradients through both the GNN (via automatic differentiation) and the PNM solver (via a discrete adjoint method), enabling fully coupled, end-to-end training. The resulting model achieves high accuracy and generalizes well across different scales, outperforming both pure data-driven and traditional PNM approaches. Gradient-based sensitivity analysis further reveals physically consistent feature influences, enhancing model interpretability. This approach offers a scalable and physically informed framework for permeability prediction in complex porous media, reducing model uncertainty and improving accuracy.

title: Unraveling water sources and groundwater discharge in Mu Us Desert lakes using coupled 222 Rn- 2 H- 18 O and hydrochemical tracers
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 675 Author(s): Fengxia Liu, Guangcai Wang, Fu Liao, Hanxiao Wang, Xinming Song, Zheming Shi, Hongyu Zhang
abstract: Desert lakes play a crucial role in sustaining hydrological and ecological equilibrium in arid regions, yet their water sources and groundwater discharge under anthropogenic pressures are not well understood. This study employed coupled hydrochemical and multi-isotopic (222Rn, δ2H, δ18O) tracers to identify water sources and estimate groundwater discharge in lakes along the eastern Mu Us Desert, an area with extensive coal mining history. Hydrochemical analysis revealed three distinct lake types: Type A (HCO3-Ca, lowest pH and EC), Type B (HCO3-Na·Ca, moderate pH and EC), and Type C (HCO3-Na, highest pH and EC), reflecting differing hydrological processes. Isotopic tracers and 222Rn mass balance modeling demonstrated that: (1) Type A lakes are predominantly recharged by shallow groundwater; (2) Type C lakes receive input from both treated and untreated coal mine drainage (CMD/TCMD); and (3) Type B lakes exhibit mixed sources of shallow groundwater and CMD/TCMD. Groundwater discharge rates were quantified at 119.47 ± 3.05 mm/d (Type A), 125.99 ± 2.43 mm/d (Type B), and 135.52 ± 11.48 mm/d (Type C). Monte Carlo simulations identified 222Rn activities (groundwater and lake water) and wind speed as the most sensitive parameters affecting discharge rate estimates. Accordingly, accurate measurement of 222Rn activity is essential for reliably determining groundwater discharge rates. Our findings provide new insights into desert lake maintenance mechanisms in mining-affected areas, offering a methodological framework for arid region hydrology studies.

title: Simulating sub-daily rainfall time series in the absence of sub-daily observations
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 675 Author(s): F. Cappelli, E. Volpi, A. Langousis, R. Deidda, S.M. Papalexiou, A. Perdios, S. Grimaldi
abstract: This paper presents a novel framework for simulating sub-daily rainfall time series in the absence of sub-daily observations, which are typically essential for calibrating conventional approaches. The proposed approach combines two classes of models: a daily rainfall model that generates long synthetic daily time series and a disaggregation model based on multifractal theory to refine the temporal resolution to sub-daily scales. The implemented procedure is parsimonious and relies solely on the observed daily rainfall time series and the power law exponent n of the intensity–duration–frequency curves, information widely available to practitioners. The framework was tested on a challenging case study consisting of 70 rain gauges in the Arno River basin (Italy), each with 20 years of continuous 15-minute rainfall data. The performance was evaluated by comparing key statistical attributes estimated from the benchmark dataset and the simulated rainfall time series at 15-minute temporal resolution, such as the dry frequency, the autocorrelation at lags 1 and 10, and the dependence of rainfall intensity on the duration of spatial averaging and return period as embodied in the well-established notion of intensity–duration–frequency (IDF) curves. The results show promising agreement, despite the limited sample size, which introduces some calibration challenges. The relative errors of the selected attributes fall within ± 15% for most of the analyzed time series, indicating that the framework offers a valuable alternative for hydrological studies, particularly in contexts where sub-daily observations are scarce or entirely absent.

title: Multimodal deep-learning–driven water-quality forecasting and scenario assessment: shifting from reactive monitoring to proactive basin management
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 675 Author(s): Zile Wang, Baiqian Shi, Paul Osmond, Kefeng Zhang
abstract: Accurately forecasting river-water quality and assessing the impacts of prospective land-use or climate interventions remain central challenges for basin managers, particularly where monitoring networks are sparse. We present a multimodal deep-learning framework that fuses static and dynamic drivers, land-use composition, population density, Köppen climate class, meteorological and hydrological variables, and air-quality indicators, within a shared representation learned by a multimodal encoder–decoder architecture that combines LSTM, Transformer, and MLP encoders with a Transformer-based decoder. Trained on > 4 million samples from 1,801 monitoring stations in China, the model achieves Nash–Sutcliffe efficiencies of 0.72–0.96 for key parameters at 3-day lead time and maintains, or improves, predictive performance at 14-day, revealing latent trends in slowly responding pollutants (e.g., total nitrogen, COD). A modular fine-tuning approach that freezes the globally pretrained encoders uses only 1% local data yet outperforms a baseline retrained with a 50/50 train–test split of the local data, underscoring strong cross-site transferability. SHapley Additive Explanations (SHAP) analyses reveal that static land-use and socioeconomic features dominate baseline water quality, while air-quality and hydro-meteorological drivers govern short-term variability through cumulative, non-linear processes. Scenario simulations further indicate that replacing built or bare land with tree cover can reduce total nitrogen by up to 60% in densely populated, high-rainfall regions. Together, these findings demonstrate a pathway from reactive monitoring to proactive basin governance: sparse observations are translated into reliable forecasts; “what-if” scenarios become quantitative pollutant-reduction estimates; and managers gain an interpretable, scalable tool to align urban growth, ecological restoration, and climate-adaptation goals.

title: An L-moments-based hypothesis test to identify homogeneous storm transposition regions
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 675 Author(s): Benjamin FitzGerald, Daniel Wright, Lei Yan, Alyssa Hendricks Dietrich, Antonia Sebastian
abstract: Deterministic storm transposition has been a longstanding component of probable maximum precipitation estimation, while stochastic storm transposition (SST) is gaining interest as a probabilistic flood hazard methodology. One example is within the Federal Emergency Management Agency’s (FEMA) National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP) to modernize methodologies for estimating flood hazard and risk throughout the United States using SST. A key challenge in the widespread and systematic application of SST is objectively delineating transposition domains, geographic regions over which rainfall is roughly homogeneous and can be transposed to accurately represent a watershed’s extreme precipitation frequency and intensity characteristics. This study introduces the spatial L-moments of annual maxima (SLAM) procedure, a novel hypothesis testing approach for defining transposition domains. SLAM assesses the similarity of L-moment statistics (L-mean, L-Coefficient of variation, L-skewness, and L-kurtosis) between a watershed’s mean annual rainfall maxima and those at transposition locations within a proposed domain. SLAM generates statistically backed homogeneous domains around each of the pilot watersheds. We found that SST-based rainfall frequency estimates using these “SLAM domains” align closely with empirical precipitation return periods for three of the four pilot watersheds, and that the domains are large enough to support the estimation of long return period rainfall. The sole exception is an NFIP pilot watershed that exhibits substantial precipitation variability due to orography. In that case, SLAM results can be interpreted as evidence that SST procedures must be adapted to be used effectively there. These results highlight the potential of SLAM to improve SST-based extreme rainfall and flood hazard assessment and to support FEMA.

title: A novel multi-link approach to drought propagation analysis using modified dynamic time warping
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 675 Author(s): Syed Bakhtawar Bilal, Vivek Gupta
abstract: Drought propagation remains poorly quantified due to the limitations of existing metrics in capturing multi-link interactions, mechanisms, and temporal dynamics driving drought evolution from meteorological to agricultural and hydrological systems. Common methods for quantifying drought propagation such as correlation, copula analysis, and causal techniques are limited by single-point comparisons that fail to represent underlying mechanisms and system complexity. In contrast, our method captures time-varying, multi-link interactions, providing a more comprehensive representation of drought propagation mechanics. This study introduces a novel adaptation of Dynamic Time Warping (DTW), a technique that aligns two time series by allowing flexible temporal shifts, to more effectively capture the dynamics of drought propagation and applies it to analyze propagation patterns across 179 catchments in southern India. The proposed method integrates a forward only propagation band with a distance matrix framework to evaluate the temporally variable linkages involved in drought development. Results reveal shifting patterns in propagation lag, likely driven by climate change, and highlight a strong dependency of lag duration on precipitation anomalies. Notably, frequency analysis of wet and dry propagation events across catchments in southern India reveals a weakening of meteorological-hydrological linkages under above-normal precipitation conditions and a strengthening under below-normal conditions. These findings highlight the utility of Modified DTW in advancing our understanding of drought behavior and its response to evolving hydroclimatic stresses.

title: Analytical solution for a slug test in an unconfined aquifer with mixed wellbore boundary conditions
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 675 Author(s): Florimond De Smedt
abstract: This study presents a novel semi-analytical solution for slug tests performed in partially screened wells in an unconfined aquifer, incorporating mixed boundary conditions at the well face. The model imposes a zero flux along the well casing and a constant pressure head over the screened interval, equal to the instantaneous water level within the well, conditions that represent the well-aquifer interaction more accurately than the generally accepted uniform flux boundary condition. The groundwater flow equations are transformed using Laplace and finite Fourier sine transformations, yielding an exact solution in the Laplace domain. Results show that, when the well screen is located far below the water table, the predicted head response in the well closely matches that obtained from traditional uniform flux models, despite significant differences in the spatial distribution of pressure head and flux along the filter. In contrast, for slug tests conducted near the water table, the uniform flux assumption introduces significant discrepancies in both simulated well responses and inferred aquifer properties. Neglecting mixed boundary effects can lead to substantial bias in estimated hydraulic conductivity, particularly near the water table where vertical flow components are important. The proposed method offers a more robust framework for interpreting slug tests in unconfined aquifers, especially when the position of the filter relative to the water table renders traditional models unreliable.

title: A multi-AI framework for accurate characterization of preferential flow pathways using a field tracer experiment
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 675 Author(s): Yanhao Wu, Haijian Xie, Mengcheng Zhang, Jiayi Hong, Mei Li, Jinzhong Wan, Tao Long, Shengtian Zhang
abstract: Accurate identification of preferential flow pathways, which are high-conductivity zones in aquifers, is essential for effective groundwater remediation. However, conventional approaches face challenges in representing non-Gaussian heterogeneity of preferential flow pathways and are computationally expensive for parameter estimation. This study proposes a novel multi-AI inversion framework to achieve efficient characterization of preferential flow pathways. Firstly, spectral normalization was applied to a Wasserstein generative adversarial network (SNWGAN) to produce high-quality structural images for non-Gaussian preferential flow pathways representation. The SNWGAN was then used to generate prior datasets for the data assimilation (DA) algorithm. By coupling SNWGAN, the DA algorithm, and numerical models simulating groundwater flow and solute transport, the numerical model-based inversion framework (SNWGAN-DA) was established for preferential flow pathways inversion. This framework was validated using a field-scale tracer experiment conducted at a chemical industrial site in northeastern China. Subsequently, an attention-enhanced convolutional network model (AEANW) was developed as a surrogate for numerical models to address computational limitations. AEANW was integrated with SNWGAN and DA to form the surrogate model-based inversion framework (SNWGAN-AEANW-DA) for efficient preferential flow pathways inversion. Finally, based on the identified preferential flow pathways, a targeted remediation layout was designed for lead contamination in the study area. The results demonstrate strong concordance between preferential flow pathways identified by the surrogate model-based inversion framework and the numerical model-based inversion framework. Excellent agreement between simulated and observed tracer data confirms the reliability of the proposed approach. After training, the AEANW surrogate model requires only 0.2 s for a single prediction, improving computational efficiency by 99% compared to the numerical model. Based on the identification results, the designed remediation scheme reduced contaminant plume migration distance by 60.5% and total exceedance area by 78.3%. The findings present a promising technical pathway for the rapid assessment and precise remediation of groundwater contamination.

title: Convolutional neural network model for rapid prediction of urban flash flood water depth and velocity maps
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 675 Author(s): Muhammad Asif, Roberto Bentivoglio, Raffaele Albano
abstract: Urbanization and climate change have intensified the need for rapid and accurate predictions of flash floods, especially in urban areas. Although numerical models produce accurate predictions, their computational cost makes them impractical for real-time simulations. Several machine learning models have been proposed as surrogates for such applications. However, most models focus only on predicting water depths and have little insight into the required variety and amount of data to train such models. In this study, we present a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) surrogate model designed to predict both water depths and flow velocities for urban pluvial flooding, using as inputs a rainfall hyetograph and seven hydro-morphological descriptors, such as aspect, curvature, slope, Manning’s roughness coefficient, topographic wetness index, flow accumulation, and digital terrain model. To train and test our approach, we considered a dataset of numerical simulations carried out using a 2D shallow-water hydrodynamic modeling in the city of Matera, Italy. For the physical-based simulations, we considered several rainfall hyetographs, either obtained from real events or derived from design scenarios for different return periods, and simulated the associated pluvial floods propagation extracting as outputs the corresponding maps of the maximum envelope of the water depths and flow velocities. The CNN model obtained a testing 0.37 cm mean absolute error (MAE), 1.7 cm root mean squared error (RMSE), and 0.80 critical success index (CSI) for water depth predictions, and 0.054 m/s MAE, 0.178 m/s RMSE, and 0.84 CSI for flow velocity predictions. The CNN model was 116.5 times faster than the physically-based hydrodynamic model using the same computational hardware. We also analyzed the effect of different combinations of rainfall events to train and validate the CNN model, showing that it benefits from a balanced dataset in terms of different return periods and presence of both synthetic and real hyetographs.
