We then employed the model to extrapolate urban flooding for higher return periods (200, 300, 500, and 1000 years), showing that the model can predict well severe extreme events, as highlighted by a high correlation between predicted maximum water volumes and total rainfall. This study contributes to the practical usability of deep learning models by providing essential support for real-time or low lead-time urban flash flood predictions, which are crucial for effective early warning and emergency management.

title: Machine learning Identifies the impacts of the Eastern route of the South-to-North water diversion Project on the transformation of dissolved organic matter
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 675 Author(s): Na Huang, Penghui Li, Yilan Jiang, Lin Chen, Dawei Wang
abstract: The spatial heterogeneity of dissolved organic matter (DOM) is synergistically modulated by hydrodynamic and aquatic chemical factors. Although several studies have suggested the DOM transformation in the influence of water diversion projects (WDPs), their real connections remain unclear. In this work, we studied the relationship between DOM transformations in recipient lakes and WDPs for the Eastern Route of the South-to-North Water Diversion Projects (ER-SNWDPs) by integrating spectral techniques, global spatial autocorrelation analysis, and machine learning analysis. The results demonstrated that DOM characteristics in recipient lakes showed spatial heterogeneity during the non-water diversion period (NWDP), whereas WDPs transformed the characteristics of DOM into a homogeneous state. A linear fitting analysis revealed that during the water diversion period (WDP), only total fluorescence intensity was dependent on water conveyance distance, while aromaticity Index, fluorescence index, and humification index, which were originally dependent on geographic characteristics, turned to be independent because of WDPs. The 3-layer Deep Neural Network model coupled with Shapley Additive Explanations analysis identified WDPs operations, conveyance distance, and nitrogen concentration as the primary drivers of DOM homogenization. Hierarchical partitioning revealed that total nitrogen replaced geographical factors as the primary contributor (15.5%) for DOM transformation during the WDP, confirming that the nitrogen variability induced by WDPs was the key factor reducing DOM spatial heterogeneity. Our study revealed the impacts of WDPs on the spatial heterogeneity of DOM in recipient lakes, providing valuable insights for the ecological risk assessment and water quality management of ER-SNWDPs.

title: An explainable physics-aware deep learning framework with improved spatiotemporal dependence matrices and signal decomposition for multi-station uncertainty daily runoff simulation
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 675 Author(s): Weiran Wu, Yan Kang, Haoyue Zhang, Libin Lin, Xinyu Zhao, Lingjie Li, Songbai Song
abstract: High-accuracy and high-timeliness efficient daily runoff simulation with strong explainability is essential for fine water resources management. However, existing single-station runoff simulation models struggle to meet basin-wide simultaneous scheduling and risk management demands due to insufficient consideration of non-stationarity, spatiotemporal dependencies, and multi-station interactions. In this paper, we propose a novel GVMD-PA-STGMD framework that integrates Variational Mode Decomposition with Grey Wolf Optimizer (GVMD), physics-aware methods (PA), and Spatiotemporal TCN-GNN-MHSA Deep-learning (STGMD) to improve multi-station daily runoff simulation in semi-arid areas. The STGMD model was developed by coupling Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN), Multi-Head Self-Attention (MHSA) and four Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to capture spatiotemporal features of multi-station runoff. In particular, the multi-station Spatio-Temporal dependence matrices were innovatively proposed for explicitly characterizing spatial interactions and nonlinear temporal dependencies across hydrological stations, thereby improving the capability of GNNs. Meanwhile, two proposed physics-aware methods—multidimensional node characteristic and node decomposition methods were introduced to STGMD for extracting meteorological influences and reservoir regulation effects on runoff processes. Furthermore, we adopted GVMD into PA-STGMD models to decompose the multi-station nonstationary daily runoff into multiple relatively stationary sub-series for enhancing the stability of input data. Finally, the iterative gradient path integrated gradients (IG2) algorithm was employed for model explainability, while Adaptive Bandwidth Kernel Density Estimation (ABKDE) was used to provide the probabilistic interval simulation. Here, the proposed framework was validated by simulating multi-station daily runoff of Wei River, China. Results show that GVMD-PA-STGMD framework achieves the best performance, and GVMD-PA-STGMD3 in the framework show distinct improvements when compared to STGMD model in terms of both NSE (36.8%) and RMSE (48.7%), and improved NSE by 19.4% and RMSE by 42.3% over the PA-STGMD models. Additionally, compared with single-station models, the proposed framework not only achieves higher simulation accuracy but also maintains superior computational efficiency, improving simulation timeliness by 38.2%. Analyses from IG2 and ABKDE further confirm its strong explainability and low uncertainty. The study demonstrates that the proposed GVMD-PA-STGMD framework with a “multi-station Spatio-Temporal dependence matrices”–“physical awareness”–“non-stationary series decomposition”–“explainability analysis” modeling process is a promising approach, which enables accurate and computationally efficient non­stationary uncertainty daily runoff simulation with strong explainability and low uncertainty.

title: Unravelling the dynamic settling behaviour of silty sediments in turbulent water
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 675 Author(s): Peng Yao, Zhongxing Qiao, Min Su, Yongping Chen, Yuan Wang, Zhengbing Wang
abstract: Bulk settling velocity is a fundamental parameter characterizing the overall settling behaviour of mixed sediment and representing the downward sediment flux in sediment transport modelling. However, the influence of turbulence on this parameter for silty sediment remains insufficiently understood. To address this, annular flume experiments were conducted using three sediment mixtures with silt contents ranging from 24% to 85% under bed shear stresses up to 1.0 Pa. Bulk settling velocities were estimated using both the conventional McLaughlin method and a novel process-approximating method based on iterative numerical simulations. Results reveal a distinct four-stage evolution. Under very weak turbulence, the settling velocity remains constant. As turbulence intensifies, the loitering effect dominates, reducing the settling velocity to a minimum near three times the critical bed shear stress of discrete particles. As turbulence further rises, the fast-tracking effect enhances, causing the velocity to gradually recover. Under strong turbulence, it increases markedly. Importantly, particle inertia affects how sediments respond to turbulence: finer, silt-rich sediment with low inertia transition between settling regimes at weaker turbulence and exhibit greater enhancement in settling velocity under strong turbulence, whereas coarser sediment with greater inertia responds more sluggishly, resulting in a more pronounced reduction by loitering. Finally, a formula was proposed to quantify bulk settling velocity as a function of bed shear stress for sediments with varying silt contents. These findings highlight that settling velocity in turbulent waters is not constant but varies with turbulence, underscoring the critical roles of turbulence and silt content in governing settling behaviour.

title: Coordinated regulation of inter-basin water transfer projects and cascade reservoirs incorporating fairness and efficiency
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 675 Author(s): Chen Niu, Jianxia Chang, Yimin Wang, Aijun Guo, Xuebin Wang, Zhehao Li
abstract: Inter-basin water transfer (IBWT) projects represent one of the most effective approaches to alleviating water scarcity caused by the uneven spatiotemporal distribution of water resources. However, the long-term sustainability of these projects critically depends on scientific regulation. Beyond addressing the inherent trade-offs between fairness and efficiency, IBWT projects must be systematically coordinated with existing cascade reservoirs in the receiving basin, rather than functioning in isolation. To this end, this study develops a nested two-layer coordinated regulation framework that integrates fairness and efficiency for IBWT projects and cascade systems. This model is applied to Phase I of the South-to-North Water Transfer Western Route (SNWT-WI) in the Yellow River Basin (YRB). Three scenarios—Basic (without the SNWT-WI), SO (standalone operation), and CO (coordinated operation)—were established for comparative analysis. Compared to the SO scenario, the CO scenario demonstrates significant advantages in securing regional water supply. Although it involves minor trade-offs regarding in-stream ecology and total power generation, the CO water transfer process is substantially more flexible. This flexibility provides superior adaptability to hydrological variability and aligns more closely with the current socio-economic development demands of the YRB. Nevertheless, the augmented inflow from the SNWT-WI increases spillway discharge, presenting a new operational challenge for existing cascade hydroelectric stations. Overall, the proposed coordinated regulation model demonstrates broad applicability, offering valuable methodological insights for the sustainable management of large-scale IBWT projects worldwide.

title: A process-informed multi-parameter downscaling framework for high-resolution source apportionment of riverine nutrients
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 675 Author(s): Xia Li, Chouai Cai, Le Fang, Cheng Zhang, Ying Peng, Qichun Yang, Ze Ren, Xinhui Liu
abstract: Eutrophication driven by excessive total nitrogen (TN) and total phosphorus (TP) poses a major threat to China’s aquatic ecosystems. Precise identification of nutrient hotspots is essential for effective mitigation but remains constrained by hydrologically mediated transport processes across multiple spatial scales. Process-based models such as the Soil and Water Assessment Tool (SWAT) are widely used, yet their coarse subbasin divisions obscure intra-subbasin heterogeneity and limit source apportionment. To address this, we developed a process-informed, multi-parameter downscaling framework integrating SWAT-derived subbasin outputs with high-resolution land use, topographic, and hydrological datasets. This approach downscaled nutrient source tracing from the SWAT subbasin scale (average ∼485 km2) to a 1 km × 1 km grid, achieving an approximately 485-fold improvement in spatial resolution, enabling fine-scale spatial patterns of TN and TP sources and revealing intra-subbasin heterogeneity that was not resolved by SWAT alone. The downscaling framework demonstrated robust performance, with calibration R adj 2 of 0.916 and 0.911 and Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency coefficient (NSE) exceeding 0.90 for log-transformed TN and TP, and leave-one-out cross-validation R adj 2 of 0.853 and 0.864, confirming strong model generalizability. Variation analysis further revealed substantial heterogeneity within the high-contributing subbasins, with 9 out of 11 for TN and 2 out of 13 for TP exhibiting internal variability over 30%. These results indicate that the downscaling analysis can uncover critical spatial variability in nutrient source distributions. Targeted interventions, such as upgrading sewage treatment and establishing constructed wetlands, should be directed to the precise internal hotspots responsible for disproportionate nutrient export. By bridging the gap between subbasin scale modeling and fine scale source delineation, this approach provides a more precise spatial representation of nutrient distributions and establishes a transferable framework for high-resolution nutrient management in diverse global watersheds.

title: Rainfall intensity and slope gradient interact to control runoff carbon–nitrogen losses and DOC–TN coupling
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 675 Author(s): Xiang Wang, Yanmin Zhao, Guoxian Huang, Wei Chen, Sichen Tong, Xiangzhou Xu, Dongfang Liang, Gang Zhou, Yuxi Nie, Yonghui Song
abstract: Rainfall intensity (I) and slope gradient (G) control carbon and nitrogen export from sloping farmlands, yet their interactive effects on dissolved organic carbon (DOC) and total nitrogen (TN) coupling are rarely quantified. Indoor rainfall simulations were conducted on sloping farmland developed on sandy-textured yellow soil using a full-factorial design (I = 40, 60, 90 mm h–1; G = 6°, 12°, 18°). Result show that runoff depth increased with I but decreased with G: on the G18, runoff depth at I90 was 2.7 times that at I40, and at I40 runoff depth at G18 was 37% lower than at G6. Two-way ANOVA showed a statistically significant I × G interaction for DOC concentration (p < 0.05), whereas TN export was mainly controlled by I. DOC export increased monotonically with I on G6 but peaked at I60 on G12–18, while runoff TN export showed an apparent optimum at I60 and TN concentrations exhibited an early-event peak. DOC–TN coupling was quantified using within-treatment DOC–TN regressions with BH–FDR adjusted q-values: G6 remained decoupled (q = 0.245–0.730; R2 ≤ 0.048); G12 showed significant positive coupling at I60–90 (q = 0.015–0.011; R2 = 0.193–0.212); and G18 showed only marginal coupling at I90 (q = 0.0519; R2 = 0.128). These results provide quantitative, state-based diagnostics of DOC–TN couplingthat go beyondstudies focusing on individual components. Therefore, different mitigation strategies are proposed for sandy-textured yellow-soil sloping farmland under comparable storm intensities: fertilizer timing should be optimized on gentle slopes, vegetated buffers should be installed at slope toes on moderate slopes, and surface protection and contour measures should be prioritized on steep slopes.

title: The processes and impacts of drought-induced extreme glacier mass loss on the south‐central Tibetan Plateau
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 675 Author(s): Derui Luo, Daijiao Lin, Yichan Xu, Meilin Zhu, Fei Zhu, Huabiao Zhao, Yang Xiang
abstract: The growing threat of reduced glacier mass to social needs and ecosystem stability is widely recognized. Extreme climate events, such as droughts or exceptionally high air temperatures, would substantially intensify glacier mass loss rate on the Tibetan Plateau (TP). However, the relationship between drought and extreme glacier mass loss on the TP, along with their impacts on lake water budgets, remains poorly understood. In this study, we analyzed the reconstructed mass balances for 853 glaciers from 1960 to 2019 in the western Nyainqentanglha Mountains on the south-central TP using glacio-meteorological observations and energy-mass balance model and found that the ablation season (June–September) drought was accompanied by extremely low precipitation and cloud cover, exceptionally high incoming shortwave radiation and relatively high air temperature, which led to extreme mass loss through decreasing albedo and snowfall, and increasing melting. Drought in the ablation season on the south-central TP may be linked to the anomalous anticyclonic circulation on the south TP and anomalous northerly flows from the south TP to the northeastern Indian subcontinent, which reduced the advection of water vapor flowing into the south-central TP from the Indian Ocean, and increased the descending motions and insolation on the south-central TP. Furthermore, the above regional atmospheric circulation anomalies were driven by a strong positive Indian Ocean dipole, a strong El Niño, a weak Indian summer monsoon, and low sea surface temperatures in the northeastern Atlantic Ocean. Moreover, in extreme mass loss years, glacier mass loss contributions to Nam Co’s summer volume increase were 1.6–4.6 times greater than in normal years. This work elucidates the physical processes underlying drought­induced extreme glacier mass loss and quantifies its critical role in driving lake level variations on the TP.

title: Non-stationary drought assessment through integration of rainfall and GRACE-based terrestrial water storage data
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 675 Author(s): Sachin Bhere, Manne Janga Reddy
abstract: Droughts, defined as prolonged periods of abnormally low rainfall and water availability, cause severe agricultural losses, water scarcity, and ecological degradation, amplifying economic and social vulnerabilities. However, most assessments rely on stationary drought indices that emphasise rainfall deficits while overlooking critical hydrological components. This study presents a novel methodology that integrates rainfall data from the India Meteorological Department (IMD) with GRACE-derived Terrestrial Water Storage (TWS) to develop the Standardised Combined TWS–Rainfall Index (SCTRI) and the Standardised Precipitation Index (SPI) under both stationary and non-stationary frameworks. Unlike stationary indices, the non-stationary counterparts incorporate evolving climatic and hydrological dynamics, enabling more robust and accurate drought assessments. The proposed indices are evaluated across 34 meteorological subdivisions of India and tested against four major drought episodes (2009, 2012, 2014–2016, and 2019). Results indicated that the SCTRI reliably captures the progression from meteorological drought (detected earlier by SPI) to hydrological and groundwater droughts, with SCTRI frequently indicating greater severity during peak phases. Non-stationary formulations of both SCTRI and SPI outperform their stationary counterparts according to standard statistical criteria, revealing longer durations and increased intensity of droughts under non-stationary conditions, particularly across the southwestern, western, and some parts of central India. Return-period analysis further indicates that non-stationarity amplifies drought persistence and severity in several meteorological zones. Overall, the findings validate the SCTRI’s applicability for historical event analysis and highlight the need for regionally targeted, proactive drought management.

title: Shifting streamflow regimes in the arctic: a multi-basin analysis using the VIC model
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 675 Author(s): Min Zhao, Xuezhi Bai, Shunqi Pan
abstract: Arctic runoff plays a crucial role in regulating the global freshwater balance, yet its long-term variability and controlling mechanisms remain insufficiently understood. This study investigates streamflow changes across six major Arctic River basins (Mackenzie, Yukon, Kolyma, Lena, Yenisei, and Ob) from 1972 to 2024, based on observational dataset analysis and simulations from the Variable Infiltration Capacity (VIC) hydrological model. Multi-scale statistical methods are applied to assess long-term trends and scale-dependent relationships between climate components and streamflow. VIC simulations further attribute these changes to shifting contributions from rainfall (Rf), evaporation (E), snow water equivalent change (ΔSWE), and soil moisture change (ΔSM), confirming a transition from snowmelt-dominated to increasingly rainfall- dominated streamflow regimes. Yukon and Kolyma exhibit early and complete regime shifts by the 2000s, whereas Lena and Mackenzie remain in transitional states. Ob exhibits a relatively stable regime with increasing rainfall influence, while Yenisei retains stronger snow-related regulation but also shows a transition toward a more mixed runoff regime. These basin-specific trajectories reveal the heterogeneous response of Arctic hydrology to ongoing warming. Evidence from this study demonstrates an ongoing transformation in Arctic hydrological processes under accelerated warming, with significant implications for freshwater export, permafrost–hydrology feedbacks, and land–atmosphere interactions in high-latitude environments.

title: Comparative analysis of JRA-3Q and JRA-55 reanalysis datasets as forcing for land surface model: implications for hydrological processes
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 675 Author(s): Zixin Wei, Fan Bai, Zhongwang Wei, Yongjiu Dai
abstract: Accurate simulation of land surface processes is important for understanding global water and energy cycles, as offline land surface models (LSMs) are heavily dependent on the quality of meteorological forcing data. The Japanese Meteorological Agency has developed JRA-3Q, a new-generation atmospheric reanalysis that succeeds JRA-55. This new dataset provides enhanced spatial resolution, improved representation of physical processes, and advanced data assimilation systems. This study evaluates the performance of JRA-3Q as forcing data for the CoLM2024 LSM, comparing it with JRA-55, with a focus on simulating hydrological processes. We conducted comprehensive model simulations from 2001 to 2010 using the False Discovery Rate (FDR) method to evaluate the statistical significance of variables and Partial Least Squares Regression (PLSR) to quantify attribution mechanisms between forcing variables and simulation outputs. Results show that JRA-3Q significantly improves the representation of precipitation, especially in arid regions, as well as air temperature, with these enhancements propagating through the LSM to improve global hydrological variables (evapotranspiration, surface soil moisture, total runoff, and streamflow). These advancements support drought detection, flood forecasting, and climate impact research. Attribution analysis reveals that hydrological improvements in arid regions benefit from enhanced precipitation accuracy. However, insufficient shortwave radiation in tropical regions limits the simulation of net radiation. Furthermore, increasing the simulation resolution does not necessarily enhance model performance, and the inclusion of dynamic leaf area index and biogeochemical modules introduces additional uncertainties, highlighting the complexity-performance trade-off. These findings emphasize the importance of regional characteristics in forcing data selection and suggest optimizing tropical radiation representation within integrated evaluation frameworks.

title: Event-based runoff-sediment response patterns and their driving mechanisms: a comparative study of typical watersheds on the Chinese Loess Plateau
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 675 Author(s): Tianning Xie, Qin Liu, Chengshuai Liu, Gan Miao, Xiaoyu Li, Runxi Li, Kejia Wen, Caihong Hu
abstract: Significant variations in event-scale runoff-sediment response mechanisms across Loess Plateau watersheds introduce substantial forecasting uncertainties. This study developed the MESH framework—encompassing flood event identification, multi-dimensional characteristic extraction, and the integration of Spearman correlation, Random Forest, sediment rating curves (SRCs), and hysteresis analysis—to investigate 104 flood events in three typical watersheds on the Chinese Loess Plateau: Baijiachuan-Zhaoshiyao (BJC-ZSY), Wuqi (WQ), and Hongde (HD). Results show BJC-ZSY follows a “high-runoff, high-sediment” regime driven by rainfall, with sediment transport strongly correlated with peak discharge (r = 0.80). Conversely, WQ and HD exhibit “low-runoff, high-sediment” characteristics with low runoff efficiency but extreme sediment concentrations averaging 279.26 kg/m3 and 591.87 kg/m3, respectively. In these sediment-abundant areas, the dominant control on sediment yield modulus shifts from peak discharge to runoff depth. SRC analysis reveals that BJC-ZSY features a low coefficient and high exponent (a = 2.52, b = 0.68), suggesting limited supply but high transport efficiency, whereas HD shows a high coefficient and low exponent (a = 161.43, b = 0.33), indicating abundant supply but lower efficiency. Hysteresis analysis identifies a mixed-source transport model in HD driven by multiple erosion processes. In contrast, counter-clockwise loops dominate in BJC-ZSY (40.0%) and WQ (44.8%), suggesting a prevalence of distal sediment sources. These findings elucidate divergent runoff-sediment relationships and internal mechanisms across the Loess Plateau, providing a scientific basis for targeted regional soil and water conservation management and a robust analytical reference for other globally significant semi-arid regions facing severe erosion.

title: Role of river network information in streamflow prediction using graph wavenet and entity-aware long short-term memory models
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 675 Author(s): Hocheol Seo, JongHyeok Lee, Suyeon Choi, Jaehee Kim, Yeonjoo Kim
abstract: Floods in river basins can develop rapidly, causing significant damage and leaving little time for an effective response. Accurate short-lead-time streamflow forecasting is thus critical for mitigating the impact of floods, particularly in densely populated or flood-prone regions. This study aimed to understand the role of river network information in predicting the streamflow using Graph WaveNet (GWNET) and entity-aware long short-term memory (EA-LSTM) models, with spatial dependencies represented by four adjacency matrices based on Euclidean or hydrological distance with or without downstream directionality. One-hour-ahead streamflow predictions were conducted based on hourly precipitation, streamflow, and water level data from 20 stations in the Yeongsangang River and Seomjingang River basins, South Korea, from 2016 to 2023. While EA-LSTM had a higher accuracy for the upstream stations, GWNET was more effective for downstream predictions, with the average Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency increasing from 0.82 for EA-LSTM to 0.89 for GWNET and the average mean absolute error decreasing from 80.35 m3/s for EA-LSTM to 59.63 m3/s for GWNET. This enhanced accuracy was attributed to the ability of GWNET to capture the physical accumulation and propagation of upstream flows through its directional graph architecture. Incorporating downstream directionality improved the performance of GWNET further, suggesting that directional connectivity plays an important role in streamflow predictions. In areas where the hydrological-to-Euclidean distance ratio exceeded 1.3, the inclusion of hydrological distance in the adjacency matrix tended to produce more accurate predictions, likely because it offered a better representation of the actual river pathways. This study demonstrated the importance of incorporating the river network structure into data-driven models and provided insights into how the spatial configuration and directional connectivity influence streamflow forecasting, which can contribute to the development of more effective early-warning systems.

title: Depth-dependent controls on soil saturated hydraulic conductivity in the Loess Plateau
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 675 Author(s): Pingping Zhang, Yunqiang Wang, Hui Sun, Ruijie Li, Jingxiong Zhou, Laiming Huang
abstract: Saturated hydraulic conductivity (Ks) is a critical parameter governing soil hydrological processes, yet most existing studies focus on upper soil layers ( 100 cm) is insufficiently characterized. This study investigated the vertical distribution, spatial variability, and controlling factors of Ks across 0–500 cm soil profiles in a small watershed on the Chinese Loess Plateau. Ks exhibited the highest values in the surface layer (0–5 cm) and decreased with depth, following power or parabolic functions (R 2 = 0.58–0.71) depending on landscape unit. Ks differed significantly among landscape units, with values ranked as tableland ≥ slope land > gully land, and significantly higher values in tableland than slope land in the 200–500 cm layer (p 20 cm), where they likely act as proxies for long-term geomorphic and pedogenic processes. These results highlight strong vertical heterogeneity in Ks and suggest that depth-explicit parameterization may improve hydrological modeling in loess regions.

title: Simulating and characterising concurrent lateral–vertical saltwater intrusion in low-lying coastal aquifers under pumping and storm-surge forcing
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 675 Author(s): Khandakar Faisal Ibn Murad, Anner Paldor, Dilip Kumar Roy, Bithin Datta
abstract: Salinisation of low-lying coastal aquifers arises via two interacting pathways—pumping-induced lateral saltwater intrusion (LSWI) and storm-surge-induced vertical saltwater intrusion (VSWI)—yet most studies model them separately, risking mischaracterisation of overall salinisation and suboptimal management. To address this gap, this study develops a fully-coupled, density-dependent surface–subsurface model that simulates the concurrent evolution and interaction of both intrusion pathways. A conceptual coastal aquifer is subjected to ten scenarios combining five pumping rates (0–200 m3/d) with either no surge or a single storm surge event over a 50-year horizon. Landward salt-mass is integrated and decomposed into LSWI, VSWI, and cross-effect components using normalised metrics. Results show that pumping is the primary control on multi-decadal salinisation and is nonlinear: stepwise increases in abstraction induce inland migration and thickening of the seawater wedge with more-than-proportional salt accumulation. A storm surge introduces an early vertical salt pulse whose magnitude and persistence increase with pumping. Without abstraction, the pulse peaks within a few years and largely flushes within ∼ two decades; with abstraction, it peaks later, decays more slowly, and at high rates leaves residual salinity that persists to year 50. Normalised analyses confirm that pumping amplifies surge impacts. Targeted comparison analyses under alternate hydraulic conductivity and recurrent-surge conditions indicate that the interaction framework remains qualitatively robust, although its expression depends on aquifer permeability and interruption of recovery by repeated flooding. Practically, the results argue for limiting overall pumping, temporarily curtailing abstraction during/after surges, and re-evaluating management interventions to avoid trapping surge-derived salinity in low-lying coastal aquifers.

title: Insights into hydrological compound dry-hot features using GNSS/GRACE-derived terrestrial water storage and land surface temperature
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 675 Author(s): Xinghai Yang, Linguo Yuan, Miao Tang, Zhongshan Jiang
abstract: Compound dry-hot events pose significantly greater threats to water security, ecological stability, and human society than individual extremes. Previous studies have primarily assessed such events by combining temperature with other meteorological variables, but these approaches fail to fully account for the compound effects of heat events and hydrological droughts induced by terrestrial water storage (TWS) deficits. Here, we define hydrological compound dry-hot events (HCDHEs) as concurrent hydrological droughts and heat extremes, and develop a novel framework for their assessment using Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) and Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment (GRACE) observations and surface temperature. First, a joint inversion model of GNSS 3D deformation and GRACE observations (G3G-JI) is proposed to estimate TWS variations in the Amazon basin. Subsequently, the standardized temperature index (STI) and TWS-based drought severity index (DSI) are integrated to construct a standardized hydrological compound index (SHCI) to quantify the severity of HCDHEs. The results demonstrate that G3G-JI outperforms GNSS-only inversion and conventional 1D GNSS-GRACE joint inversion models, more accurately restoring the local TWS signals along the Amazon River. Comparisons of various indices show that SHCI effectively captures heat and hydrological drought characteristics, with correlation coefficients of 0.8 for both STI and DSI. Analyses of the Amazon sub-basins show that 7–15 HCDHEs occur during 2008–2022, with maximum durations of 16–30 months. Additionally, SHCI successfully captures the spatial evolution characteristics of HCDHEs and exhibits strong consistency with the meteorological standardized compound event index (SCEI). Our study introduces a geodesy-based novel framework to assess the compound characteristics of heat and hydrological droughts, expanding the application of GRACE and GNSS in assessing global and regional compound extreme events.

title: Arsenic cycling driven by hydrogeochemical-tidal coupling in a sandy subterranean estuary
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 675 Author(s): Wenli Xia, Long Gao, Jiawei Liu, Yiqing Wang, Zijun Wu
abstract: Submarine groundwater discharge (SGD) represents a significant but often poorly quantified pathway for terrestrial contaminants, such as arsenic (As), to the coastal ocean. This study investigates As dynamics in a subtropical sandy subterranean estuary (STE) located in Beihai, China. Our findings reveal that recirculated saline groundwater discharge (RSGD) dominates the seaward flux of As. Although dissolved As concentrations remain below the WHO guideline (<10 μg L−1) throughout the STE, the total SGD-derived As flux (0.25 ± 0.03 kg d−1) exceeds combined inputs from local rivers. The STE functions as both a filter and a conduit for As. Within the intertidal zone, the Upper Saline Plume (USP) facilitates seaward As transport from the mixing zone via tidal recirculation, while sediments at its base effectively remove terrestrially derived As through Fe-Si-As coprecipitation and adsorption onto iron oxides. Tidal pumping is the key driver, simultaneously intensifying the oxic conditions that enable this near-shore As sequestration and promoting seawater-groundwater exchange that sustains reducing conditions in deeper recirculation zones. In these anoxic zones, As mobility is regulated by Mn-oxide reductive dissolution and competitive anion exchange (notably with silicate and phosphate), which also controls As(III)/As(V) speciation. This work establishes STE as the dominant pathway for terrestrial As to the coastal ocean in this system. We propose a conceptual model that integrates tidal hydrodynamics with redox and adsorption geochemistry to explain As cycling in sandy STEs, providing a critical framework for predicting and managing As dynamics in vulnerable coastal systems worldwide.

title: Effects of temporary streamflow interruption on hyporheic oxygen dynamics
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 675 Author(s): Alejandra Villa, Shai Arnon, Stephanie Spahr, Cara Beume, Jörg Lewandowski
abstract: Short-term streamflow interruptions, i.e. brief recessions of surface water resulting in temporary drying of streams, are occurring more frequently nowadays due to climate change or water management operations. The impact of these streamflow disruptions on hyporheic oxygen dynamics and their legacy effect on stream metabolism remains unclear. This study aims to investigate the effects of a one-day streamflow interruption on oxygen patterns in surface water and the hyporheic zone by comparing conditions before and after the disturbance. We monitored oxygen concentrations in surface water and streambed sediment of a side channel of the River Erpe (Berlin, Germany) at different experimentally manipulated surface water velocities (0.1–0.5 ms−1) for five days before and fifteen days after the streamflow interruption. After rewetting, the diel amplitude of surface water oxygen concentrations decreased by 30% relative to pre-interruption conditions, and partially recovered within five days. Oxygen concentrations in deeper sediment layers were lower than before the interruption. This response pattern was observed across all surface water velocities (0.1–0.5 m s−1), and it was more pronounced at 0.4 and 0.1 ms−1. Three weeks after flow resumed, surface water and porewater oxygen concentrations remained around 2 mgL−1 lower than pre-interruption values. Five days after the disturbance, a gradual metabolic response was observed, with gross primary production and ecosystem respiration increasing in magnitude by 26% and 31%, respectively. These findings emphasize that short streamflow intermittency can trigger shifts in oxygen regimes and metabolism, and therefore needs to be accounted for in sustainable water management strategies.

title: Integrating an improved SWAT model and geochemical constraints to assess climate change impacts on hydrological processes and extremes in mixed karst and non-karst basin
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 675 Author(s): Chujie Bu, Jie Niu, Haiyang Hao, XingXing Cao, Pan Wu
abstract: Climate change poses significant challenges to hydrological processes, particularly in mixed karst and non-karst basin. This study develops a SWAT-Duliujiang model to simulate hydrological processes in the Duliujiang River Basin, integrating a three-reservoir module for karst subbasins and geochemical constraints. The three-reservoir structure better represents karst aquifer dynamics, while model calibration divided subbasins into four groups based on geological background, with outputs constrained by regional geochemical signatures to ensure realistic simulations. Driven by bias-corrected 6th International Coupled Model Comparison Program (CMIP6) multi-model ensemble data under four Shared Socio-economic Pathways (SSP) scenarios (SSP1-2.6, SSP2-4.5, SSP3-7.0, and SSP5-8.5), the study projects hydrological responses across near-term (2015–2040), mid-term (2041–2070), and long-term (2071–2100) periods. The results show that the SWAT-Dliujiang model significantly improves the accuracy of hydrological simulations, and the incorporation of geochemical constraints effectively avoids outputs that are inconsistent with actual conditions. Across all scenarios, both streamflow and sediment yield increase significantly, with sediment yield exhibiting more pronounced spatial heterogeneity than streamflow. Compared with the historical period (2010–2017), the most pronounced changes in hydrological processes occur in the downstream region during the wet season under the long-term SSP5–8.5 scenario. Specifically, under this scenario, the long-term annual streamflow is projected to reach 43.76 m3/s, and the annual sediment yield is projected to reach 1579.35 × 103tons/month, which are 1.09 and 7.8 times the historical period values, respectively. Future annual maximum monthly streamflow (AMMS) is expected rise by 13%–57% in the long-term relative to the near-term. Random Forest analysis reveals distinct driving mechanisms: AMMS in karst regions are primarily controlled by wet season precipitation and groundwater, whereas non-karst regions are dominated by wet season precipitation. This study underscores the necessity of integrating geochemical constraints into hydrological process simulations in complex geological settings and highlights the importance of adopting region-specific adaptive strategies for water resources management and hydroclimatic extremes mitigation under climate change.

title: Driving factors of urban reclaimed water development in water-environment-sensitive regions: Coupled causal inference with double machine learning and causal forest
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 675 Author(s): Chuanyi Wang, Fengping Wu, Xiangzeng Shi, Wentong Yang, Xinyu Liu
abstract: Amid global water scarcity and ecological pressures, reclaimed water has become a key pathway to improving efficiency and alleviating water stress. Yet the causal mechanisms and heterogeneous responses remain underexplored. This study develops a six-dimension indicator system and advances a coupled double machine learning–causal forest framework, embedding city and year fixed effects to control unobservable heterogeneity and enhance robustness in causal inference. Using the Beijing–Tianjin–Hebei urban agglomeration as a case, nine core drivers are identified, including reclaimed water investment, per capita disposable income, pipeline length, and water sector employment, suggesting the importance of infrastructure conditions and underlying socioeconomic context. Cities exhibit distinct responses: resource-dominant cities show diminishing marginal returns, while peripheral cities display latecomer advantages. Development effects also reveal “high-efficiency windows” followed by “attenuation phases”, which may be associated with policy timing and urban development stages. These findings offer methodological innovation and practical guidance for differentiated, dynamic reclaimed water strategies.

title: G2Lcast: A global-to-local adversarial network for high-fidelity precipitation nowcasting
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 675 Author(s): Chuanhao Yin, Huawang Qin, Xiangming Zheng
abstract: Nowcasting of precipitation is pivotal for socioeconomic activities and public safety; yet, achieving high-fidelity forecasts remains fundamentally challenged by the multi-scale spatiotemporal complexity of rainstorms. Existing deep-learning models struggle to reconcile local detail preservation with global dependency modeling and are plagued by a systematic blurry prediction bias: they consistently underestimate the intensity of convective extremes and yield overly smoothed fields. To address these deficiencies, we introduce G2Lcast, a non-autoregressive generative adversarial framework founded on a global-to-local hierarchical evolution principle. Specifically, we devise a wavelet-based information-preserving codec coupled with an energy bypass that injects low-frequency energy components directly into the latent temporal evolution, guaranteeing structural fidelity at every forecast step. The core G2Lmixer module disentangles global filters in the frequency domain, independently modulates amplitude and phase spectra, and synergizes with multi-scale spatial convolutions to approximate spatiotemporal dependencies in linear complexity. The entire predictor is trained adversarially: a discriminator enforces the generator to synthesize precipitation fields that are statistically and visually indistinguishable from observations, thereby mitigating the inherent blurriness. Extensive evaluations on two public benchmarks demonstrate G2Lcast’s superiority. On KNMI, it raises the mean CSI by 6.17% over the best prior art; on SEVIR, its skill in predicting extreme convection (CSI-219) surges by 35.88%. These results establish a new state-of-the-art for precipitation nowcasting and underscore G2Lcast’s broad potential for complex spatiotemporal forecasting tasks.

title: Simultaneous calibration of hydraulic head and deformation data for characterizing vertical aquitard heterogeneity via geostatistical inverse modeling
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 675 Author(s): Yue Zhuo, Jinguo Wang, Weihua Liu, Weijian Li, Walter A Illman, Chao Zhuang
abstract: In multi-aquifer-aquitard systems, sustained and intensive groundwater extraction and recharge can induce both elastic and inelastic deformation in aquitards. Because aquitards are commonly heterogeneous, accurately characterizing the spatial distributions of hydraulic conductivity (Kv ), elastic skeletal specific storage (Sske ), and inelastic skeletal specific storage (Sskp ) is essential for understanding aquitard drainage and deformation. In this study, the COMPAC model was used to generate synthetic hydraulic head and deformation responses in a thick aquitard under varying hydraulic head conditions in adjacent aquifers. A quasi-linear geostatistical approach (QLGA) was then applied to characterize aquitard heterogeneity in Kv , Sske and Sskp through joint calibration of hydraulic head and deformation data. Seven synthetic cases were designed to examine the effects of the initial hydraulic head observation point, the hydraulic head observation interval, and cumulative deformation zonation on inversion performance. The results show that the initial hydraulic head observation point mainly affects the estimated Kv field, whereas the hydraulic head observation interval and cumulative deformation zonation primarily influence the estimated Sske field. A smaller hydraulic head observation interval leads to poorer Sske inverse quality, while a more detailed deformation zonation markedly improves it. By contrast, the corresponding changes in Kv and Sskp are comparatively limited. Overall, an appropriate observation design for hydraulic head and deformation can improve inversion performance while reducing unnecessarily dense monitoring. This provides a reliable basis for characterizing vertical aquitard heterogeneity and offers quantitative guidance for optimizing observation design.

title: Multiscale discrete fracture-matrix method for simulating groundwater flow in fractured geological media
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 675 Author(s): Chen Zuo, Lei Ma, Di Gao, Qiankun Luo, Yaping Deng, Jiazhong Qian
abstract: Fractured geological media (FGM) are characterized by inherent multiscale features and strong spatial heterogeneity. When simulating groundwater flow in FGM, existing methods encounter a critical challenge in balancing accuracy against efficiency. This study proposes a novel Multiscale Discrete Fracture-Matrix (MsDFM) method. The method employs a hybrid modeling strategy that combines explicit, embedded, and implicit representations of different-scale fractures. Large-scale fractures that influence macroscopic flow are explicitly represented using matching meshes within the rock matrix, while the numerous and geometrically complex medium-scale fractures are represented by non-matching meshes that are embedded within the matrix domain. The two types of meshes are connected using the Coupling Finite Element Method, and the hydraulic head continuity between the fracture and matrix is enforced weakly via a penalty term. The performance of this method is evaluated using commercial software and various published methods in a series of calculation examples. In comparison with the benchmark cases, the results of this method matched well with those of 14 methods, and the number of fracture elements is reduced by 40%. The comparison with the DFN proved that this method can simulate the influence of a permeable matrix on local fracture water flow. Furthermore, comparison with MFEPM proves that MsDFM not only avoids local numerical errors caused by pseudo-connectivity, but also improves the calculation time by 8.7 times. The results show that the proposed method significantly reduces computational cost while ensuring high accuracy, providing a reliable and highly scalable new method for the accurate and efficient simulation of FGM.

title: From puddles to lakes: hydrological and colloidal controls on element transport in peatland surface waters
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 675 Author(s): Bogdan A. Mikhaleiko, Sergey N. Vorobyev, Danil G. Kurashev, Yuri Y. Kolesnichenko, Artem G. Lim, Rinat M. Manasypov, Larisa G. Kolesnichenko, Sergey N. Kirpotin, Oleg S. Pokrovsky
abstract: Despite extensive knowledge of Siberian lake biogeochemistry during the open-water period, seasonal dynamics of small peatland water bodies remain poorly constrained. We investigated organic and inorganic nutrients and major and trace solutes, including ∼ 40 trace elements in peatland pools of the Great Vasyugan Mire (western Siberia), the world’s largest mire, across a size gradient from ephemeral spring puddles to permanent lakes > 1 km2 and through four hydrological seasons: post-ice-off spring, late summer, pre-ice autumn, and winter under ice. We hypothesized that small, hydrologically isolated pools would be dominated by organic-matter inputs and trace-element enrichment, whereas larger lakes would show stronger groundwater influence. Consistent with this framework, organic nutrients, and lithogenic trace elements increased with decreasing pool size, while larger lakes exhibited lower DOC aromaticity, higher pH, and elevated concentrations of labile inorganic solutes, including anions and alkali and alkaline-earth metals. Across seasons, concentrations of most dissolved constituents increased by a factor of 1.3–2.0 from spring to winter, indicating progressive winter accumulation and selective ice-induced fractionation. The smallest (<100 m2) pools showed peak spring DOC and associated Zn, Mn, and Cr concentrations, reflecting leaching from flooded mosses and vascular plants together with snowmelt inputs of atmospherically deposited elements. During spring and summer, 50–80% of dissolved alkali and alkaline-earth metals occurred in colloidal form (1 kDa–0.45 µm). Overall, peatland pool hydrochemistry reflects the combined influence of surface biomass leaching, peat-derived subsurface inflow, groundwater inputs, and atmospheric deposition; climate-driven increases in thaw season length and hydrological connectivity may enhance solute mobilization and transfer to downstream waters.

title: Integrating multi-isotope fingerprinting with machine-learning-informed Bayesian mixing reveals agricultural dominance of phosphorus sources in a River basin
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 675 Author(s): Anqi Guo, Xuemei Chen, Junxi Yang, Jie Qin, Yuepeng Yin, Peng Wang, Ningtao Wang, Wen Zhang
abstract: Precise identification and quantification of phosphate sources are essential for preventing eutrophication in river basins. Multi-isotope approaches, including phosphate oxygen isotopes (δ18Op), nitrogen isotopes (δ15N), and carbon isotopes (δ13C), are well-established for phosphate source tracing, but their quantitative estimates may be biased relative to actual source contributions. We integrated δ18Op, δ15N, and δ13C isotopes into a unified machine-learning coupling framework to quantitatively refine phosphate source tracing and constrain the inferential uncertainty inherent in multi-isotope mixing models. Qualitative multi-isotope fingerprinting identified Agricultural Phosphorus Sources (APS) as dominant, and the multi-isotope-Stable Isotope Mixing Models in R (SIMMR) apportionment under ML-informed priors yielded a posterior mean contribution of 56.11% for APS, with Phosphate Rock & Chemical Industry, Domestic Sewage, and Endogenous Release contributing 12.97%, 12.83%, and 18.09%, respectively. XGBoost accurately predicted total phosphorus in surface water (R2 = 0.76). SHAP (Shapley Additive Explanations) analysis identified agriculture-related pressure indicators (Agri-Fishery GDP, arable area, and phosphate fertilizer production) as the principal positive predictors of total phosphorus concentration. We further translated SHAP signals into a SHAP-based Agricultural Pressure Index to elicit weakly informative Dirichlet priors for SIMMR, narrowing 95% credible interval widths by 8.60–23.19% and shifting APS upward (mean 49.81%→56.11%), with minor reshuffling among secondary sources. This study integrates multi-isotope fingerprinting with a machine-learning-constrained SIMMR model to improve phosphorus-source apportionment.

title: Daily stream water temperature modeling and forecasting for ungaged watersheds at the CONUS scale
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 675 Author(s): Daniel Philippus, Claudia R. Corona, Terri S. Hogue
abstract: Stream water temperature (SWT) affects both societal and ecosystem functions, with impacts ranging from dissolved oxygen to algal blooms to lotic species mortality. The role of SWT in water chemistry and ecology has motivated rapid development in SWT modeling. Large-domain models support evaluation of current and future SWT conditions and impacts of disturbances or restorations across varied spatiotemporal scales, particularly for ungaged watersheds (no SWT observations). In the last decade, daily/kilometer-resolution, ungaged SWT models have been developed for the contiguous United States (CONUS), but do not support forecasting. Existing SWT forecasting models are constrained by lower spatial/temporal resolution or are applicable to smaller domains. Thus, there is a need for higher-resolution, large-domain forecasting to investigate future thermal conditions at scale. We present the first CONUS-scale, kilometer-resolution, forecasting-capable, daily, ungaged SWT model: “temperature estimation: near-term expected temperatures” (TempEst-NEXT). TempEst-NEXT can account for changing surface conditions (e.g., urbanization) and climate and is demonstrated for historical prediction and 1–16 day forecasting. TempEst-NEXT is also compatible with NOAA’s NextGen National Water Model framework. Forecast-forced historical tests (two-day lead) for mean daily SWT show a median RMSE of 2.3 ∘ C (2.1 ∘ C with estimated weather inputs), R 2 of 0.92, and bias of 2.0% for ungaged watersheds, with similar performance in real-time forecasts (1–16 day lead). Unlike comparable SWT models, TempEst-NEXT forecasts do not require local calibration, supporting real-time decision-making for water-resource management, such as reservoir releases, where long-term observations are unavailable. Broadly, TempEst-NEXT enables efficient, flexible, large-scale prediction of stream thermal regimes.

title: Hundred-year changes in water and sediment in the Inner Mongolia reach of the Yellow River: trend transitions, driving mechanisms, and attribution quantification
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 675 Author(s): Jiatao Wu, Xiaomin Liu, Tingxi Liu, Anjun Deng, Hai Huang
abstract: Under the combined effects of climate change and human activities, the water–sediment processes in the Yellow River Basin demonstrate significant evolutionary characteristics. Based on long-series hydrological and sediment data from the Inner Mongolia reach of the Yellow River collected between 1919 and 2024, this article investigates the water–sediment relationship using trend-sudden change-cycle identification and segmental diagnosis methods. Combined with data on reservoir construction and operation, land use, and vegetation index, it analyses the mechanisms driving changes at different phases and quantifies the contribution rate of each factor. The results obtained include: (1) Runoff and sediment transport on a centennial scale generally exhibited a significant decreasing trend (p < 0.01). Compared with the high flow and sediment period P2 (1933–1967), the average annual runoff at various stations during the multi-reservoir coordinated operation period P6 (2014–2024) decreased by 7.0–28.6%, while sediment transport decreased by 62.7–90.7%, with an even more significant reduction during the flood season. (2) The runoff volume changed abruptly in 1933, 1969, and 1986, and an additional abrupt change in sediment transport occurred in 2000, which coincided with the construction period of upstream hydraulic engineering. A cycle analysis showed that there were 38a, 14a, and 7a cycles in the runoff, while the sediment transport presented multi-scale fluctuation characteristics of 2-4a, 7-14a, 22-24a, and 46a. (3) The water–sediment relationship underwent a significant transition from a natural dominant phase (P1, P2) to a phase driven by both human activities and climate after 1968. Subsequently, human activities became the major factor influencing the modern water–sediment process, with contributions of more than 55% to runoff and more than 79% to sediment transport. (4) The construction of cascade reservoirs had a significantly stronger effect on sediment transport (mainly during the flood season) than on runoff. From 1980 to 2020, the expansion of forest land (+10.8%) and grassland (+1.3%) contributed to sediment reduction. On the other hand, the expansion of construction land (+37.1%) and the continuous increase in the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) (0.026/10a) led to an increase in evapotranspiration and ecological water use, which became significant factors in runoff reduction. This study reveals the driving mechanisms of water–sediment changes in the Inner Mongolia reach from both long-term and multi-phase perspectives. These results may serve as a quantitative reference for the water–sediment regulation and ecological protection of the Yellow River basin.

title: Improving extreme runoff simulation with spatially optimized Fengyun satellite precipitation
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 675 Author(s): Yuehua Ran, Kunlong He, Xiaohong Chen, Haojie Li
abstract: To tackle the challenge of extreme runoff simulation in data-limited hydrological regions, this study introduces a novel approach to enhance runoff simulation accuracy in the typical humid basin in China by integrating the Soil and Water Assessment Tool (SWAT) sub-basin delineation into the XGBoost model. We optimized sub-basin precipitation extraction and basin-scale aggregation methods to improve accuracy of extreme runoff simulation. The Fengyun Quantitative Precipitation Estimation (FY QPE) was validated for its potential in hydrological modeling, and SHAP analysis was employed to quantify the contributions of driving factors, revealing the underlying mechanisms of hydrological elements. Representative precipitation sequences were extracted using mean values (FYm) and hybrid maximum-mean strategies (FYmm70, FYmm75, FYmm80, FYmm85, FYmm90, FYmm95) tailored to extreme runoff thresholds. Five aggregation methods—Mean, Area-weighted (A), Distance-to-Center (D2C), Distance-to-Outlet (D2O), and Cluster—were explored to derive basin-scale precipitation inputs, bridging distributed and lumped modeling for enhanced stability and interpretability. Results show FY QPE correlates highly with in-situ data (CC > 0.87, NSE > 0.74), despite underestimating extremes. XGBoost outperforms SWAT with an 10% NSE improvement and reduced PBIAS. FYmm80 and FYmm85 excel in extreme high runoff simulation (PBIAS improvement >20%), while D2C and D2O aggregation methods yield the best overall performance (NSE 0.80–0.82, KGE 0.81–0.86). Cumulative precipitation (7-day and 15-day) as the dominant driver, with seasonal variations influenced by humidity and sunshine duration. This framework advances satellite-driven hydrological modeling by improving precipitation spatial representativeness, reducing biases in extremes, and enhancing model explainability.

title: Divergent pattern and trends of water color in global river mouths revealed by decadal Landsat observations
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 675 Author(s): Liuhong Huang, Xiaomei Fan, Lin Huang, Shichang Gao, Chunqiao Song
abstract: River mouths serve as critical interfaces linking terrestrial and marine systems, where water color integrates signals of watershed processes, human activities, and hydrodynamic conditions. However, the complex interplay of river discharge and optical constituents necessitates effective remote sensing monitoring. The Forel-Ule Index (FUI), a 21-scale colorimetric classification, offers effective robust indicator of water quality. This study quantifies the spatial patterns, decadal trends, and seasonal variability of water color across 3,209 global river mouths using Landsat-8 imagery from 2013 to 2024. The results show that global river mouths exhibited a mean FUI of 17.76 ± 2.65, with substantial spatial heterogeneity. High FUI values were predominantly observed in, densely populated low-latitude regions (e.g., Southeast Asia, western Central America), while lower values were observed in Arctic coastal regions and the mid-latitude areas of the Northern Hemisphere. Small river mouths generally showed higher FUI than large ones due to limited dilution capacity, with regional exceptions in the Southeast Asia, Amazon, West Africa and West North America. Over the past decade, global FUI displayed a slight overall increase, with rising trends prevailing in the Arctic and low-latitude Southern Hemisphere, contrasting with declines in mid-latitudes. Seasonally, FUI peaked in summer and reached a minimum in winter. Notably, nearly 30% of river mouths exhibited negative trends across seasons, particularly in summer and winter, whereas persistent increases were mainly concentrated in eastern Australia. This study provides a global assessment of river-mouth water color dynamics, revealing the distinct scale effects and regional disparities in river mouth water quality. It is expected to offer critical scientific evidence for understanding land–ocean interactions under the dual drivers of climate change and anthropogenic perturbations.

title: Buffering of perennial flow and differential response of adjacent sub-catchments under a drying climate
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 675 Author(s): Rose-Anne Bell, John Nikolaus Callow, Sarah A. Bourke
abstract: Rivers in the Southern Hemisphere mid-latitudes are particularly sensitive to climate-induced flow regime changes. Yet process-based studies on hydrological resilience under drying climates remain limited, especially at sub-catchment scales. This paper addresses these gaps through a hydrological analysis of three adjacent sub-catchments in southwest Western Australia’s high-rainfall forested region, which exhibit non-uniform responses to decreasing rainfall. The study area has experienced stepwise drying since the 1930–40s and 1960–70s with overall rainfall reductions of 10–28% at long-term gauges in surrounding catchments. To investigate streamflow responses and identify groundwater-mediated mechanisms buffering or sustaining perennial flow, we analysed long-term streamflow records and identified periods in the record where streams had undergone a hydrological change. To do this, we characterised dry season flow trends, identified statistical changepoints in rainfall and streamflow records, and analysed variations in streamflow yield (rainfall-runoff conversion) across hydrological seasons. Results reveal sustained streamflow decline across all sub-catchments amid rainfall reductions. However, while two streams transitioned to ephemeral and seasonally dry flow regimes (with statistical changepoints in 1975 and 2001), the third adjacent stream retained perennial flow, attributed to lower aridity and potentially landscape and hydrogeological features that enhance catchment storage and groundwater support. This work highlights subtle differences in climatic independence among adjacent sub-catchments, suggesting forms of hydrological resilience through groundwater buffering.

title: Interactive effects of vegetation and water regimes on evaporative fraction from two coastal wetland ecosystems
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 675 Author(s): Qiong Han, Tiejun Wang, Qinling Bai, Cong-Qiang Liu
abstract: Understanding land surface energy partitioning is critical to predict water and energy processes; however, its regulation mechanism remains unclear in coastal wetlands with complex landscapes and alternating hydrological regimes. Here, daily evaporative fraction (EF) was contrasted for Phragmites australis and Suaeda salsa in a brackish coastal wetland from northern China with a focus on the roles of groundwater and standing water. Daily EF was observed to range from 0.008 to 0.93 (averaged at 0.23) and 0.009 to 0.58 (0.14) at the Phragmites australis and Suaeda salsa sites, respectively. Net radiation and air temperature were primarily correlated with EF at both sites, while the influences of other variables (e.g., depth to groundwater table-DTGT and canopy conductance) varied with growing stages and water regimes. Differences in the EF controlling factors between the sites were consistent with their contrasting rooting depths and soil moisture. In early growing seasons with drought, EF showed a negative relationship with DTGT below critical DTGT thresholds (∼0.95 m for Phragmites australis and ∼ 0.73 m for Suaeda salsa). The larger threshold for Phragmites australis was associated with its deeper root system and drier soils. In the mid-growing season with inundation, standing water depth positively influenced EF while EF became less responsive to DTGT after the inundation with reduced vegetation activities. Our study suggests interactive effects of vegetation and water regime on EF dynamics within this coastal wetland ecosystem, which may have important implications in the context of future climate change with more frequent extreme weather events.

title: Observation of urban karst flows inform planning, design and construction of green stormwater infrastructure
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 675 Author(s): Kathryn M. Boening-Ulman, R. Andrew Tirpak, Jay F. Martin, Alessandra S. Braswell, William F. Hunt, Ryan J. Winston
abstract: Rapid increases in population worldwide have led to an expansion of areas characterized by highly connected impervious surfaces. Located beneath these surfaces are intertwined layers of infrastructure, such as pipes, gravel-filled trenches, and wires, transporting utilities and water. Engineers have increasingly adopted infiltrating stormwater control measures (SCMs) to more closely mimic pre-development hydrology and mitigate the detrimental effects of impervious cover on receiving waters. When constructing SCMs, there is the potential for stormwater to unintentionally discharge via alternate pathways along subsurface infrastructure, particularly when retrofitting into existing urban developments which requires disturbing the subgrade and potentially relocating utilities. Interactions between infiltrated stormwater and this complex system of subsurface infrastructure, or the ‘urban karst’ phenomena, are an anthropogenic corollary to the natural tunnels and underground channels that can be found in geologies with highly soluble rock such as limestone. Relatively few studies have explored the impacts of urban karst pathways on the performance of infiltrating SCMs. This study explored three SCMs with known urban karst interactions in Ohio and North Carolina (USA) to better understand the potential impacts of urban karst SCMs. Alternate drainage pathways were confirmed using methods such as long-term monitoring, sewer inspection cameras, and dye tracer studies. Recommendations for design techniques, such as impenetrable liners in SCM installations, that could be implemented to minimize the urban karst effect are also explored. Given potential unintended consequences of urban karst and the prevalence of underground infrastructure worldwide, engineers are encouraged to consider these techniques in all SCM designs.

title: GRHyMoLAP: A process-driven ODE catchment hydrology model inspired by GR4J and HyMoLAP approaches
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 675 Author(s): Sianou Ezéckiel Houénafa, Melissa Latella, Lionel Cédric Gohouede, Cenk Sezen
abstract: Catchment hydrology can be represented using ordinary differential equations (ODEs), offering strong interpretability through a transparent and structured formulation. However, few ODE models, including the Hydrological Model based on the Least Action Principle (HyMoLAP), explicitly govern runoff evolution or fully leverage hydro-climatic inputs across diverse catchments. In this work, we introduce GRHyMoLAP, a process-driven, quasi-physical hybrid model with 4 parameters, that integrates the production store of the Génie Rural à 4 paramètres Journalier (GR4J) into the HyMoLAP framework, yielding an ODE formulation that replaces GR4J’s routine for simulating runoff dynamics. This integration produces a single, streamlined framework that eliminates the need for separate pre-simulations. Validated across 222 CAMELS-AUS and 671 CAMELS-US catchments, GRHyMoLAP consistently outperforms the original HyMoLAP in 98.6% and 97.2% of cases, respectively, reflecting its improved ability to balance immediate rainfall effects with internal catchment processes and deal with non-linearities. While average predictive accuracy is comparable to the GR4J and Hydrologiska Byråns Vattenbalansavdelning (HBV) models, GRHyMoLAP generally demonstrates enhanced robustness in low-performing catchments, under low-flow and extreme runoff ratio conditions, mainly due to its greater ability to capture recession dynamics. Sensitivity analysis using the Sobol method and uncertainty analysis within the Generalized Likelihood Uncertainty Estimation (GLUE) framework indicate that the parameters controlling recession shape ( μ ) and input scaling ( γ ) are the most influential. Owing to its distinctive formulation, GRHyMoLAP can serve as a complementary approach to HyMoLAP and GR4J. Moreover, its structure opens up opportunities for further developments, highlighting its potential as a versatile tool for water resources management.

title: Robustness of correlation coefficient-based information criterion for characterizing short- and long-term dependence of hydroclimatic time series
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 675 Author(s): Jingqun Huo, Yan-Fang Sang, Ping Xie, Vijay P. Singh
abstract: Dependence amongst hydroclimatic processes is an inherent and important characteristic, and accurate determination of the optimal order of dependence models is required for describing hydroclimatic dependence characteristics, but it is a challenging issue. The coefficient-based information criterion (CCIC) was proposed for determining the optimal model order, however, its comparative advantage to other methods for handling short- as well as long-term dependence models has not been clarified. In this study, we first mathematically proved the asymptotical consistency of the CCIC method, and then systematically investigated the efficiency of determining the optimal order for both short- and long-term dependence models by seven methods, considering the influences of seven main factors and their interaction effects. Results of Monte-Carlo experiments and observed precipitation data analysis validated the higher accuracy of the CCIC method for determining the optimal model order compared to other six methods used widely, and also showed its robustness for handling both short-term and long-term dependence models. Comparatively, the AICc (Akaike Information Criterion with correction) and BIC (Bayesian Information Criterion) method gave acceptable order-determination accuracy; however, the HQIC (Hannan-Quinn Information Criterion), FPE (Final Prediction Error), AIC (Akaike Information Criterion), and SVD (singular value decomposition) methods exhibited low accuracy and are therefore not recommended. It is noted that the standard AICc method is theoretically suboptimal for handling symmetric moving average (SMA) models, due to the incompatibility of its bias-correction derivation with the SMA covariance structure. Consequently, the CCIC method is recommended for determining the optimal order of dependence models, however, the factors of data length, mean value, and signal-to-noise ratio of the hydroclimatic time series to be analyzed should be carefully checked and handled in practical applications of the method.

title: Hybrid-cryo: a modular data-physics hybrid framework for cryospheric runoff simulation
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 675 Author(s): Zijie Tang, Jianyun Zhang, Mengliu Hu, Hossein Hashemi, Feifei Yuan, Kang Xie, Zhongrui Ning, Cuishan Liu, Mingming Xie, Jiangjiang Zhang, Guoqing Wang
abstract: Climate warming profoundly alters cryospheric hydrological cycles, exacerbating the challenge of simulating the poorly understood processes, particularly in complex, glacier- and permafrost-dominated headwater basins. This difficulty centers on accurately representing the compound runoff regimes generated by the complex, overlapping interactions between rainfall and multiple cryospheric melt processes. These overlapping processes yield highly nonlinear and state-shifting runoff responses, making cold-region hydrological simulation particularly challenging. To address this, we introduce Hybrid-Cryo, a modular data-physics hybrid framework for cryospheric runoff simulation, guided by a “skeleton-and-muscles” design philosophy. The framework’s physical “skeleton” reformulates process-based models (PBMs) into a differentiable architecture to enforce physical consistency and generate key hydrological states. Its adaptive “muscles”, comprising deep learning components, then learn the complex runoff dynamics from these states while correcting for the skeleton’s inherent biases. We evaluated the proposed framework in two major headwater basins on the Tibetan Plateau: the source regions of the Yangtze River (SRYZ) and the Yellow River (SRYE), benchmarking it against a suite of conventional PBMs, a standalone Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), and other physics-guided deep learning (PGDL) approaches. Results show that the proposed approach outperformed all benchmark models, with test Kling-Gupta Efficiency (KGE) of 0.925 (SRYE) and 0.883 (SRYZ). The proposed framework also showed promising transferability to data-scarce upstream sub-basins with local fine-tuning. Analysis using Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) uncovered the proposed framework’s internal problem-solving strategy, revealing that it learns to dynamically down-weight the contributions of poorly performing physical modules.

title: Young water proportion characteristics and influencing factors of large-scale basins: insights from long-term and high-frequency water sampling
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 675 Author(s): Yong Zhang, Xinping Zhang, Xuhong Zhan, Chengcheng Xia, Jinzhao Liu, Zhiguo Rao, Xinguang He, Keshao Liu, Zhu Liu, Xiong Xiao
abstract: Climate change has increased extreme weather events, making understanding river response vital for water management. This study conducted a 15-year daily and 5-day sampling of precipitation and river water in Changsha from 2010 to 2025. By integrating in-situ isotopic measurements with hydrometeorological data from the Xiangjiang River Basin (XRB), isoGSM2-simulated precipitation, we applied multiple methods to estimate the young water fraction (Fyw) and assessed uncertainties. The results indicated that: (1) The XRB experienced warming and drying trends, leading to isotopically enriched river water due to enhanced evaporative fractionation within the basin storage water. (2) Our resampling experiment revealed that standard monthly sampling introduced over two-fold uncertainty in the estimations of Fyw compared to the 5-day sampling. Long-term high-frequency sampling is thus essential for constraining model uncertainty. (3) Influenced by precipitation, Fyw(Q) estimated for high-discharge intervals demonstrated higher accuracy (e.g., 90–95%, 95–100%, and Top 2.5%, with adjusted R2 of 0.66, 0.66, and 0.71, respectively). This result provided direct empirical evidence for an efficient young water transport process in the XRB during heavy precipitation events. (4) Global synthesis indicated that in humid monsoon regions, the Fyw is primarily driven by precipitation intensity. Short-duration heavy precipitation activates transient preferential flow pathways, allowing young water to bypass the large and older water storage in larger basins. This mechanism explains why, in large monsoon basins during wet years, the observed Fyw at a higher level than expected. Overall, this study identifies the impact of changes in hydrometeorological factors on Fyw within the XRB.

title: Snow phenology-guided regionalization for parameter optimization: enhancing runoff simulation in an alpine basin
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 675 Author(s): Yu Shi, Xiongpeng Tang, Zhanliang Zhu, Chao Gao, Xin Yin, Silong Zhang
abstract: Alpine basins are critical sources of freshwater for downstream regions, with their hydrology largely shaped by intricate snow dynamics. However, spatial snow heterogeneity challenges accurate runoff simulation in traditional hydrological models. This study aims to improve the runoff simulation accuracy of the Variable Infiltration Capacity (VIC) hydrological model in alpine basins by proposing a snow phenology-guided regional parameterization framework. The framework integrates remote sensing-based snow phenology data with PCA-K-means clustering for basin regionalization, introduces a spatially heterogeneous calibration strategy to enhance parameter representation, and constructs a surrogate model based on representative cells to reduce parameter dimensionality. The application in the Source Region of the Yellow River Basin (SYRB) demonstrated: (1) The regionalization method effectively identified three distinct snow phenology clusters. (2) The spatially heterogeneous calibration strategy outperformed the traditional approach, achieving a Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE) of 0.83 with a relative error (RE) of 8.59%, which represents a relative enhancement in dynamic simulation accuracy over the traditional baseline (NSE = 0.73, RE = 6.03%). A pronounced performance contrast was observed during snow seasons (Nov-Apr): NSE = 0.81, RE = − 0.75% (baseline: NSE = 0.54, RE = 2.36%). (3) The surrogate modeling approach retained competitive performance during both the full period (NSE = 0.83, RE = 14.34%) and snow seasons (NSE = 0.68, RE = 13.16%) while significantly reducing parameter dimensionality. The framework provides an effective solution for enhancing runoff simulation capability in SYRB, yielding valuable insights into hydrological processes and offers insights for water‑resources management in similar regions globally.

title: Is the Weibull distribution reliable to describe the rainfall kinetic power and momentum in Mediterranean environments?
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 675 Author(s): F.G. Carollo, R. Caruso, V. Ferro, M.A. Serio
abstract: Understanding the characteristics of the rainfall drop size distribution (DSD) at the land surface is crucial for elucidating the mechanisms of precipitation that affect soil erosion processes.
